The Legislature has already carved large holes in that process. In June 2025, as part of the budget, Governor Newsom signed (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2025/06/30/governor-newsom-signs-into-law-groundbreaking-reforms-to-build-more-housing-affordability/) AB 130 and SB 131. AB 130 exempts from CEQA entirely infill housing on sites of up to 20 acres in cities or urban areas that are consistent with local zoning. SB 131 exempts day care centers, federally qualified health centers, food banks, advanced manufacturing facilities, wildfire risk-reduction projects, broadband in local rights of way, certain water projects and housing-element rezonings, and creates a "near-miss" rule under which a project that fails an exemption on a single condition is reviewed only for the effects of that condition. The Governor continued in September 2026, signing CEQA bills for fire stations (AB 2152), hospitals (AB 2231), day care zoning (SB 299), geothermal exploration (AB 2234) and an urban rail station (SB 1375), while vetoing (https://www.gov.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Veto-Message-SB-954.pdf) SB 954, which would have narrowed the advanced-manufacturing exemption: the exemption "should be given a meaningful opportunity to work," he wrote.
Prop 45 is different in kind. The 2025 laws exempt specific project types from CEQA; Prop 45 exempts nothing but rewrites the procedure for everything in its nine categories, regardless of size, from a four-unit infill lot to a transmission line, and it does so by initiative, which the Legislature can amend only by a two-thirds vote "consistent with, and furthers the purposes of, this chapter," after the bill has been in print for 12 business days. Prop 45 also incorporates AB 130's labor rule, applying prevailing-wage requirements to housing "solely to buildings over 85 feet in height."
Proposition 45 is replacing CEQA's open-ended review and litigation timelines with fixed clocks and narrower court remedies for nine categories of essential projects, as the measure's text and the Legislative Analyst's Office describe in October 2026. The clocks: 30 days to accept an application, 365 business days to decide an EIR
The measure's first mechanism is deadlines with consequences. Under section 21017, an agency has 30 days to tell an applicant whether an application is complete, with "an exhaustive written corrections list"; if it misses the deadline, "the initial application shall be deemed complete." An application cannot be rejected for lacking studies that were not on a published checklist, and the agency "shall not request or require an applicant to provide any new information unless that information was included on the exhaustive written corrections list."
Sections 21018 and 21019 then set the review clock: a final decision on an environmental impact report "no later than 365 days after" the application is complete, 180 days for a negative declaration, and 90 days to decide that a project is exempt or already covered by a prior review. Those three clocks run in business days, excluding weekends and state holidays; every other deadline in the chapter is in calendar days. The applicant can extend them. The LAO notes that current law also has time limits, but "nothing specific happens if an agency misses" them.
Under Prop 45 something does. Section 21020 lets an applicant, once a deadline passes, demand a meeting or hearing within 60 days at which the agency "shall" make "a final written determination on the available environmental review documentation that has been completed as of the date of the meeting or hearing" and "a final written determination to approve or disapprove the essential project." Compliance with the deadlines is "a nondiscretionary ministerial duty," and the applicant may sue within 90 days to enforce it. The agency keeps the power to say no: "No outcomes on any proposed essential project are preordained by this chapter."
The review: One alternative, standards frozen at filing, comment capped
The second mechanism narrows what the review contains. Section 21025 provides that "the applicant shall develop one proposed alternative to the essential project," which need not be at a different site, and that the EIR "shall only analyze" the project, that alternative and the no-project option; "all additional alternatives beyond those described… are unnecessary." The applicant's alternative "shall be presumed to lessen impacts that the alternative is intended to address" if substantial evidence supports it. Under current law, the LAO says, "the lead agency must develop and consider a range of reasonable alternatives to the project or its location."
Section 21022 fixes the yardstick: impacts are assessed "based on compliance with existing laws," defined as rules "in effect on the date an application for an essential project was submitted," with exceptions for later rules an agency finds necessary to avoid "a specific, adverse life-safety impact" and for building and fire code updates. Section 21021 caps public comment at 20 days for a negative declaration and 45 for a draft EIR, allows extensions only "by a court of competent jurisdiction," bars reopening the period at later hearings, and provides that comments outside those windows, other than oral testimony at a recorded hearing and late comments on issues that could not have been raised earlier, "shall be disregarded and excluded from the administrative record." Current law sets minimum comment periods, not maximums.
Tribal consultation changes too. For essential projects, "California Native American tribe" is redefined to mean a "consulting tribe," one "that appears on the most recent list published by the United States" of federally recognized tribes and is "traditionally and culturally affiliated with the geographic area." The LAO's letter (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250480.pdf) to the Attorney General describes the effect: consultations would be based "on the list of federally recognized tribes, rather than on the longer contact list maintained by the state Native American Heritage Commission." The measure sets its own consultation procedure, with a records search within 20 days and a 30-day response window, and makes agreed mitigation "enforceable conditions of project approval."
The courts: 30 days to sue, 270 to decide, and no power to void the approval
The third mechanism is litigation. Section 21027 requires a CEQA challenge to an essential project to be filed "within 30 days" of the notice of determination and "completed within 270 days, inclusive of original and appellate court proceedings," extendable by up to 90 days at the court's discretion. Section 21026 limits the claims a petitioner can bring to "a public agency's noncompliance with objective existing laws," where objective means "involving no personal or subjective judgment and being uniformly verifiable by reference to an external and uniform benchmark," and limits the court to asking "whether the approval or authorization is supported by substantial evidence in light of the whole record." The LAO's summary of the contrast: "Under current law, the court can use its independent judgment to determine whether an agency appropriately applied CEQA."
The remedy is the sharpest change. If a court finds a violation, "the remedy shall be limited only to prohibiting commencement of the noncomplying part, phase, or activity until the noncompliance is corrected"; "a court may not order or direct… that a public agency rescind its approval," and parts of the project outside the deficiency "shall not be subject to the writ."
A full injunction is available only "upon a showing by clear and convincing evidence that an essential project would have a specific, adverse impact upon public safety" with no feasible mitigation. The administrative record is confined to documents the agency published and to timely comments. Once an approval survives challenge, or the agency files its return to the writ, "no further action or proceeding to challenge the implementation through completion of construction" may be filed. The provisions apply to cases "pending on, or commenced after" the effective date, which, as an initiative, is the fifth day after the Secretary of State certifies the result on December 11.
The measure contains no attorney-fee provision; its only reference to attorneys is a clause directing the Attorney General to appoint independent counsel, with a continuous appropriation, if the Governor and Attorney General decline to defend the act in court.
The cost: High tens of millions a year at first, uncertain after
The LAO's ballot analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm) estimates that "during the first several years, Proposition 45 likely would increase costs for the state and local governments, including state courts," at "the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially exceeding $100 million annually," partly covered by fees on applicants and litigants. Its December 2025 letter had put the same costs at "tens of millions of dollars annually for the first several years" and added that "over the long term… state and local governments likely would experience net savings due to reduced administrative and legal workload," with court effects ranging "from annual savings of up to the tens of millions of dollars to annual costs of up to the low tens of millions."
The ballot analysis is more cautious about the long term, "uncertain, but potentially more significant," in either direction, depending on "how the new procedures change the number of eligible projects that get built and whether those projects have different environmental impacts." It also carries the sentence the No campaign quotes: some agencies "might incur costs to mitigate or respond to" projects approved with "unintended negative environmental impacts."
Proposition 45's author and funders: Nielsen Merksamer, CalChamber and a $226 million committee
The proponent of record is Kurt R. Oneto, a partner at the Sacramento election-law firm Nielsen Merksamer, whose firm bio (https://www.nmgovlaw.com/team/kurt-oneto/) says he "has served as counsel and legal strategist to over 60 ballot measure campaigns." The Attorney General's list (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives/active-measures) shows Oneto as proponent of three measures on this ballot: Prop 45 and the two tax measures, Props 41 and 42, that could cancel the billionaire tax. The California Chamber of Commerce says (https://advocacy.calchamber.com/2026/09/11/calchamber-board-of-directors-announces-positions-on-november-ballot-measures/) it "not only strongly supports Proposition 45… but led the effort to qualify the measure"; the Secretary of State's top-funder disclosure (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/top-funders/2000-top-funders-04-01-26.pdf) for the petition drive names a CalChamber-sponsored committee with "major funding from" Building a Better California, Edison International and the California Building Industry Association.
Building a Better California is the committee behind the campaigns against Prop 40 and for Props 41 and 42, the three measures that decide the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/). Its Cal-Access filings show $226.7 million raised between January 1 and September 19, 2026; the FPPC identifies its top donors as Google co-founder Sergey Brin and venture capitalist L. John Doerr III; it has no public website, and its filer telephone number is that of Nielsen Merksamer's San Rafael office. It has given $10 million to the Yes on 45 committee, the largest single contribution on that side.
The FPPC's October 6 list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/) puts the Yes side at $32.8 million from top contributors across three committees: after Building a Better California come the California Building Industry Association's issues committee ($5.65 million, with KB Home and Lennar as its top donors) and the association itself ($2.25 million), a separate CBIA committee funded by homebuilders ($4.1 million), a committee funded by PG&E ($2.4 million), CalChamber ($2 million), Edison International ($2 million), the California Association of Realtors ($1.5 million), a business PAC funded by California Resources Corporation and PG&E ($1.35 million), and $500,000 each from the hospital association, California Resources Corporation and a committee sponsored by Prologis, the logistics real-estate company. The No side reports $22.2 million: Clean and Healthy California, an environmental political committee, $7.08 million; philanthropist Wendy Schmidt, $5 million; the State Building and Construction Trades Council's committees, $2 million; the Laborers, $1.5 million; Operating Engineers Local 12 and the Iron Workers, $1 million and $1.5 million; and the Center for Biological Diversity, Earthjustice and the Natural Resources Defense Council's action fund in smaller amounts.
The lineup is unusual. The construction trades, which generally support building, are against; so are the Laborers, whose members build the projects the measure covers. The No argument's explanation is the measure's labor provisions and its backers: it "was written by the California Chamber of Commerce and financed by gas and electric utilities and corporate PACs." The Yes argument's coalition includes the California Children's Hospital Association, the California Water Association, American Clean Power, LULAC, the NAACP state conference and the California Taxpayers Association.
The arguments: Red tape versus review
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/arguments-rebuttals.htm) is an affordability case: "Permitting delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new home," it says, and Prop 45 "will help lower rents and mortgages." The campaign's own site (https://yesonprop45.com/) adds a commissioned estimate that the measure would raise housing permitting 18.1% and "add nearly 200,000 homes over ten years." It stresses that "Prop. 45 does not exempt a single project from environmental review" and that "cities and counties retain full authority to approve or deny projects."
The No argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/arguments-rebuttals.htm) is a public-health case: Prop 45 "lets projects move forward with far less scrutiny of their harms to air, water and public health," and "reduces public agency requirements to consider public comments." Its campaign site (https://www.noprop45ca.com/) argues the measure "would fast-track polluting projects like data centers, pipelines, and industrial warehouses." Data centers, pipelines and warehouses are not among the nine categories; the measure's definition does include, for every essential project, "all related and ancillary public, private, and utility infrastructure," and whether that clause lets parts of such projects use the track is a reading the campaigns dispute and the text does not settle. The $75,000, 200,000-home and 639-day figures on the Yes side come from a report the campaign commissioned; all of these are claims, printed in the guide with the standard note that arguments "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
Polling and endorsements on Proposition 45
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of 1,103 likely voters, reading the ballot title, found 49% yes, 46% no and 5% undecided, inside the ±3.8-point margin. No other independent poll has published a Prop 45 result. McClatchy's California editorial board, writing for the Sacramento Bee and four other papers, endorsed (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317475362.html) the measure on October 5; the Bakersfield Californian has also endorsed it; the San Francisco Chronicle's editorial board lists its Prop 45 recommendation as "coming soon," and the Los Angeles Times had not published one as of October 12. The parties have split: the California Democratic Party opposes (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 45 and the California Republican Party supports (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it. Governor Newsom, whose campaign released his positions on 12 of the 14 measures on October 9, has not taken one (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/) on Prop 45; he is "still reviewing" it and Prop 41, his spokesperson told the San Francisco Chronicle (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php).
Proposition 45 after November 3: An immediate rewrite of pending reviews, amendable only by two-thirds
If Prop 45 passes, it takes effect on certification and applies "to all pending and future public agency and judicial review and processes for all essential projects," so applicants with reviews under way could withdraw and resubmit under the new chapter, and pending lawsuits would be subject to its litigation rules. The Legislature could adjust it only by a two-thirds vote that "furthers the purposes" of the chapter. If it fails, CEQA continues as the Legislature has been reshaping it since 2025, exemption by exemption. Either way, Proposition 45 is the first time California voters have been asked to decide the shape of environmental review directly, and the question on the ballot is not whether to review essential projects but how long, how deeply, and with what recourse.

Under section 21017, an agency has 30 days to tell an applicant whether an application is complete, with "an exhaustive written corrections list"; if it misses the deadline, "the initial application shall be deemed complete." An application cannot be rejected for lacking studies that were not on a published checklist, and the agency "shall not request or require an applicant to provide any new information unless that information was included on the exhaustive written corrections list."
Sections 21018 and 21019 then set the review clock: a final decision on an environmental impact report "no later than 365 days after" the application is complete, 180 days for a negative declaration, and 90 days to decide that a project is exempt or already covered by a prior review. Those three clocks run in business days, excluding weekends and state holidays; every other deadline in the chapter is in calendar days. The applicant can extend them. The LAO notes that current law also has time limits, but "nothing specific happens if an agency misses" them.
Under Prop 45 something does. Section 21020 lets an applicant, once a deadline passes, demand a meeting or hearing within 60 days at which the agency "shall" make "a final written determination on the available environmental review documentation that has been completed as of the date of the meeting or hearing" and "a final written determination to approve or disapprove the essential project." Compliance with the deadlines is "a nondiscretionary ministerial duty," and the applicant may sue within 90 days to enforce it. The agency keeps the power to say no: "No outcomes on any proposed essential project are preordained by this chapter."
The review: One alternative, standards frozen at filing, comment capped
The second mechanism narrows what the review contains. Section 21025 provides that "the applicant shall develop one proposed alternative to the essential project," which need not be at a different site, and that the EIR "shall only analyze" the project, that alternative and the no-project option; "all additional alternatives beyond those described… are unnecessary." The applicant's alternative "shall be presumed to lessen impacts that the alternative is intended to address" if substantial evidence supports it. Under current law, the LAO says, "the lead agency must develop and consider a range of reasonable alternatives to the project or its location."
Section 21022 fixes the yardstick: impacts are assessed "based on compliance with existing laws," defined as rules "in effect on the date an application for an essential project was submitted," with exceptions for later rules an agency finds necessary to avoid "a specific, adverse life-safety impact" and for building and fire code updates. Section 21021 caps public comment at 20 days for a negative declaration and 45 for a draft EIR, allows extensions only "by a court of competent jurisdiction," bars reopening the period at later hearings, and provides that comments outside those windows, other than oral testimony at a recorded hearing and late comments on issues that could not have been raised earlier, "shall be disregarded and excluded from the administrative record." Current law sets minimum comment periods, not maximums.
Tribal consultation changes too. For essential projects, "California Native American tribe" is redefined to mean a "consulting tribe," one "that appears on the most recent list published by the United States" of federally recognized tribes and is "traditionally and culturally affiliated with the geographic area." The LAO's letter (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250480.pdf) to the Attorney General describes the effect: consultations would be based "on the list of federally recognized tribes, rather than on the longer contact list maintained by the state Native American Heritage Commission." The measure sets its own consultation procedure, with a records search within 20 days and a 30-day response window, and makes agreed mitigation "enforceable conditions of project approval."
The courts: 30 days to sue, 270 to decide, and no power to void the approval
The third mechanism is litigation. Section 21027 requires a CEQA challenge to an essential project to be filed "within 30 days" of the notice of determination and "completed within 270 days, inclusive of original and appellate court proceedings," extendable by up to 90 days at the court's discretion. Section 21026 limits the claims a petitioner can bring to "a public agency's noncompliance with objective existing laws," where objective means "involving no personal or subjective judgment and being uniformly verifiable by reference to an external and uniform benchmark," and limits the court to asking "whether the approval or authorization is supported by substantial evidence in light of the whole record." The LAO's summary of the contrast: "Under current law, the court can use its independent judgment to determine whether an agency appropriately applied CEQA."
The remedy is the sharpest change. If a court finds a violation, "the remedy shall be limited only to prohibiting commencement of the noncomplying part, phase, or activity until the noncompliance is corrected"; "a court may not order or direct… that a public agency rescind its approval," and parts of the project outside the deficiency "shall not be subject to the writ."
A full injunction is available only "upon a showing by clear and convincing evidence that an essential project would have a specific, adverse impact upon public safety" with no feasible mitigation. The administrative record is confined to documents the agency published and to timely comments. Once an approval survives challenge, or the agency files its return to the writ, "no further action or proceeding to challenge the implementation through completion of construction" may be filed. The provisions apply to cases "pending on, or commenced after" the effective date, which, as an initiative, is the fifth day after the Secretary of State certifies the result on December 11.
The measure contains no attorney-fee provision; its only reference to attorneys is a clause directing the Attorney General to appoint independent counsel, with a continuous appropriation, if the Governor and Attorney General decline to defend the act in court.
The cost: High tens of millions a year at first, uncertain after
The LAO's ballot analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm) estimates that "during the first several years, Proposition 45 likely would increase costs for the state and local governments, including state courts," at "the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially exceeding $100 million annually," partly covered by fees on applicants and litigants. Its December 2025 letter had put the same costs at "tens of millions of dollars annually for the first several years" and added that "over the long term… state and local governments likely would experience net savings due to reduced administrative and legal workload," with court effects ranging "from annual savings of up to the tens of millions of dollars to annual costs of up to the low tens of millions."
The ballot analysis is more cautious about the long term, "uncertain, but potentially more significant," in either direction, depending on "how the new procedures change the number of eligible projects that get built and whether those projects have different environmental impacts." It also carries the sentence the No campaign quotes: some agencies "might incur costs to mitigate or respond to" projects approved with "unintended negative environmental impacts."
Proposition 45's author and funders: Nielsen Merksamer, CalChamber and a $226 million committee
The proponent of record is Kurt R. Oneto, a partner at the Sacramento election-law firm Nielsen Merksamer, whose firm bio (https://www.nmgovlaw.com/team/kurt-oneto/) says he "has served as counsel and legal strategist to over 60 ballot measure campaigns." The Attorney General's list (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives/active-measures) shows Oneto as proponent of three measures on this ballot: Prop 45 and the two tax measures, Props 41 and 42, that could cancel the billionaire tax. The California Chamber of Commerce says (https://advocacy.calchamber.com/2026/09/11/calchamber-board-of-directors-announces-positions-on-november-ballot-measures/) it "not only strongly supports Proposition 45… but led the effort to qualify the measure"; the Secretary of State's top-funder disclosure (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/top-funders/2000-top-funders-04-01-26.pdf) for the petition drive names a CalChamber-sponsored committee with "major funding from" Building a Better California, Edison International and the California Building Industry Association.
Building a Better California is the committee behind the campaigns against Prop 40 and for Props 41 and 42, the three measures that decide the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/). Its Cal-Access filings show $226.7 million raised between January 1 and September 19, 2026; the FPPC identifies its top donors as Google co-founder Sergey Brin and venture capitalist L. John Doerr III; it has no public website, and its filer telephone number is that of Nielsen Merksamer's San Rafael office. It has given $10 million to the Yes on 45 committee, the largest single contribution on that side.
The FPPC's October 6 list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/) puts the Yes side at $32.8 million from top contributors across three committees: after Building a Better California come the California Building Industry Association's issues committee ($5.65 million, with KB Home and Lennar as its top donors) and the association itself ($2.25 million), a separate CBIA committee funded by homebuilders ($4.1 million), a committee funded by PG&E ($2.4 million), CalChamber ($2 million), Edison International ($2 million), the California Association of Realtors ($1.5 million), a business PAC funded by California Resources Corporation and PG&E ($1.35 million), and $500,000 each from the hospital association, California Resources Corporation and a committee sponsored by Prologis, the logistics real-estate company. The No side reports $22.2 million: Clean and Healthy California, an environmental political committee, $7.08 million; philanthropist Wendy Schmidt, $5 million; the State Building and Construction Trades Council's committees, $2 million; the Laborers, $1.5 million; Operating Engineers Local 12 and the Iron Workers, $1 million and $1.5 million; and the Center for Biological Diversity, Earthjustice and the Natural Resources Defense Council's action fund in smaller amounts.
The lineup is unusual. The construction trades, which generally support building, are against; so are the Laborers, whose members build the projects the measure covers. The No argument's explanation is the measure's labor provisions and its backers: it "was written by the California Chamber of Commerce and financed by gas and electric utilities and corporate PACs." The Yes argument's coalition includes the California Children's Hospital Association, the California Water Association, American Clean Power, LULAC, the NAACP state conference and the California Taxpayers Association.
The arguments: Red tape versus review
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/arguments-rebuttals.htm) is an affordability case: "Permitting delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new home," it says, and Prop 45 "will help lower rents and mortgages." The campaign's own site (https://yesonprop45.com/) adds a commissioned estimate that the measure would raise housing permitting 18.1% and "add nearly 200,000 homes over ten years." It stresses that "Prop. 45 does not exempt a single project from environmental review" and that "cities and counties retain full authority to approve or deny projects."
The No argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/arguments-rebuttals.htm) is a public-health case: Prop 45 "lets projects move forward with far less scrutiny of their harms to air, water and public health," and "reduces public agency requirements to consider public comments." Its campaign site (https://www.noprop45ca.com/) argues the measure "would fast-track polluting projects like data centers, pipelines, and industrial warehouses." Data centers, pipelines and warehouses are not among the nine categories; the measure's definition does include, for every essential project, "all related and ancillary public, private, and utility infrastructure," and whether that clause lets parts of such projects use the track is a reading the campaigns dispute and the text does not settle. The $75,000, 200,000-home and 639-day figures on the Yes side come from a report the campaign commissioned; all of these are claims, printed in the guide with the standard note that arguments "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
Polling and endorsements on Proposition 45
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of 1,103 likely voters, reading the ballot title, found 49% yes, 46% no and 5% undecided, inside the ±3.8-point margin. No other independent poll has published a Prop 45 result. McClatchy's California editorial board, writing for the Sacramento Bee and four other papers, endorsed (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317475362.html) the measure on October 5; the Bakersfield Californian has also endorsed it; the San Francisco Chronicle's editorial board lists its Prop 45 recommendation as "coming soon," and the Los Angeles Times had not published one as of October 12. The parties have split: the California Democratic Party opposes (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 45 and the California Republican Party supports (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it. Governor Newsom, whose campaign released his positions on 12 of the 14 measures on October 9, has not taken one (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/) on Prop 45; he is "still reviewing" it and Prop 41, his spokesperson told the San Francisco Chronicle (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php).
Proposition 45 after November 3: An immediate rewrite of pending reviews, amendable only by two-thirds
If Prop 45 passes, it takes effect on certification and applies "to all pending and future public agency and judicial review and processes for all essential projects," so applicants with reviews under way could withdraw and resubmit under the new chapter, and pending lawsuits would be subject to its litigation rules. The Legislature could adjust it only by a two-thirds vote that "furthers the purposes" of the chapter. If it fails, CEQA continues as the Legislature has been reshaping it since 2025, exemption by exemption. Either way, Proposition 45 is the first time California voters have been asked to decide the shape of environmental review directly, and the question on the ballot is not whether to review essential projects but how long, how deeply, and with what recourse.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, the FPPC contributor list as of October 6, 2026, endorsements as of October 12, 2026, and polling fielded through September 10, 2026.

When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). The DSF-based sampling frame used for address selection is enhanced with a series of refinements—such as the appendage of various ancillary d

," and "if the court finds that the agency did not follow CEQA correctly, it can stop the whole project."
The Legislature has already carved large holes in that process. In June 2025, as part of the budget, Governor Newsom signed (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2025/06/30/governor-newsom-signs-into-law-groundbreaking-reforms-to-build-more-housing-affordability/) AB 130 and SB 131. AB 130 exempts from CEQA entirely infill housing on sites of up to 20 acres in cities or urban areas that are consistent with local zoning. SB 131 exempts day care centers, federally qualified health centers, food banks, advanced manufacturing facilities, wildfire risk-reduction projects, broadband in local rights of way, certain water projects and housing-element rezonings, and creates a "near-miss" rule under which a project that fails an exemption on a single condition is reviewed only for the effects of that condition. The Governor continued in September 2026, signing CEQA bills for fire stations (AB 2152), hospitals (AB 2231), day care zoning (SB 299), geothermal exploration (AB 2234) and an urban rail station (SB 1375), while vetoing (https://www.gov.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Veto-Message-SB-954.pdf) SB 954, which would have narrowed the advanced-manufacturing exemption: the exemption "should be given a meaningful opportunity to work," he wrote.
Prop 45 is different in kind. The 2025 laws exempt specific project types from CEQA; Prop 45 exempts nothing but rewrites the procedure for everything in its nine categories, regardless of size, from a four-unit infill lot to a transmission line, and it does so by initiative, which the Legislature can amend only by a two-thirds vote "consistent with, and furthers the purposes of, this chapter," after the bill has been in print for 12 business days. Prop 45 also incorporates AB 130's labor rule, applying prevailing-wage requirements to housing "solely to buildings over 85 feet in height."
Proposition 45 is replacing CEQA's open-ended review and litigation timelines with fixed clocks and narrower court remedies for nine categories of essential projects, as the measure's text and the Legislative Analyst's Office describe in October 2026. The clocks: 30 days to accept an application, 365 business days to decide an EIR
The measure's first mechanism is deadlines with consequences. Under section 21017, an agency has 30 days to tell an applicant whether an application is complete, with "an exhaustive written corrections list"; if it misses the deadline, "the initial application shall be deemed complete." An application cannot be rejected for lacking studies that were not on a published checklist, and the agency "shall not request or require an applicant to provide any new information unless that information was included on the exhaustive written corrections list."
Sections 21018 and 21019 then set the review clock: a final decision on an environmental impact report "no later than 365 days after" the application is complete, 180 days for a negative declaration, and 90 days to decide that a project is exempt or already covered by a prior review. Those three clocks run in business days, excluding weekends and state holidays; every other deadline in the chapter is in calendar days. The applicant can extend them. The LAO notes that current law also has time limits, but "nothing specific happens if an agency misses" them.
Under Prop 45 something does. Section 21020 lets an applicant, once a deadline passes, demand a meeting or hearing within 60 days at which the agency "shall" make "a final written determination on the available environmental review documentation that has been completed as of the date of the meeting or hearing" and "a final written determination to approve or disapprove the essential project." Compliance with the deadlines is "a nondiscretionary ministerial duty," and the applicant may sue within 90 days to enforce it. The agency keeps the power to say no: "No outcomes on any proposed essential project are preordained by this chapter."
The review: One alternative, standards frozen at filing, comment capped
The second mechanism narrows what the review contains. Section 21025 provides that "the applicant shall develop one proposed alternative to the essential project," which need not be at a different site, and that the EIR "shall only analyze" the project, that alternative and the no-project option; "all additional alternatives beyond those described… are unnecessary." The applicant's alternative "shall be presumed to lessen impacts that the alternative is intended to address" if substantial evidence supports it. Under current law, the LAO says, "the lead agency must develop and consider a range of reasonable alternatives to the project or its location."
Section 21022 fixes the yardstick: impacts are assessed "based on compliance with existing laws," defined as rules "in effect on the date an application for an essential project was submitted," with exceptions for later rules an agency finds necessary to avoid "a specific, adverse life-safety impact" and for building and fire code updates. Section 21021 caps public comment at 20 days for a negative declaration and 45 for a draft EIR, allows extensions only "by a court of competent jurisdiction," bars reopening the period at later hearings, and provides that comments outside those windows, other than oral testimony at a recorded hearing and late comments on issues that could not have been raised earlier, "shall be disregarded and excluded from the administrative record." Current law sets minimum comment periods, not maximums.
Tribal consultation changes too. For essential projects, "California Native American tribe" is redefined to mean a "consulting tribe," one "that appears on the most recent list published by the United States" of federally recognized tribes and is "traditionally and culturally affiliated with the geographic area." The LAO's letter (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250480.pdf) to the Attorney General describes the effect: consultations would be based "on the list of federally recognized tribes, rather than on the longer contact list maintained by the state Native American Heritage Commission." The measure sets its own consultation procedure, with a records search within 20 days and a 30-day response window, and makes agreed mitigation "enforceable conditions of project approval."
The courts: 30 days to sue, 270 to decide, and no power to void the approval
The third mechanism is litigation. Section 21027 requires a CEQA challenge to an essential project to be filed "within 30 days" of the notice of determination and "completed within 270 days, inclusive of original and appellate court proceedings," extendable by up to 90 days at the court's discretion. Section 21026 limits the claims a petitioner can bring to "a public agency's noncompliance with objective existing laws," where objective means "involving no personal or subjective judgment and being uniformly verifiable by reference to an external and uniform benchmark," and limits the court to asking "whether the approval or authorization is supported by substantial evidence in light of the whole record." The LAO's summary of the contrast: "Under current law, the court can use its independent judgment to determine whether an agency appropriately applied CEQA."
The remedy is the sharpest change. If a court finds a violation, "the remedy shall be limited only to prohibiting commencement of the noncomplying part, phase, or activity until the noncompliance is corrected"; "a court may not order or direct… that a public agency rescind its approval," and parts of the project outside the deficiency "shall not be subject to the writ."
A full injunction is available only "upon a showing by clear and convincing evidence that an essential project would have a specific, adverse impact upon public safety" with no feasible mitigation. The administrative record is confined to documents the agency published and to timely comments. Once an approval survives challenge, or the agency files its return to the writ, "no further action or proceeding to challenge the implementation through completion of construction" may be filed. The provisions apply to cases "pending on, or commenced after" the effective date, which, as an initiative, is the fifth day after the Secretary of State certifies the result on December 11.
The measure contains no attorney-fee provision; its only reference to attorneys is a clause directing the Attorney General to appoint independent counsel, with a continuous appropriation, if the Governor and Attorney General decline to defend the act in court.
The cost: High tens of millions a year at first, uncertain after
The LAO's ballot analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm) estimates that "during the first several years, Proposition 45 likely would increase costs for the state and local governments, including state courts," at "the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially exceeding $100 million annually," partly covered by fees on applicants and litigants. Its December 2025 letter had put the same costs at "tens of millions of dollars annually for the first several years" and added that "over the long term… state and local governments likely would experience net savings due to reduced administrative and legal workload," with court effects ranging "from annual savings of up to the tens of millions of dollars to annual costs of up to the low tens of millions."
The ballot analysis is more cautious about the long term, "uncertain, but potentially more significant," in either direction, depending on "how the new procedures change the number of eligible projects that get built and whether those projects have different environmental impacts." It also carries the sentence the No campaign quotes: some agencies "might incur costs to mitigate or respond to" projects approved with "unintended negative environmental impacts."
Proposition 45's author and funders: Nielsen Merksamer, CalChamber and a $226 million committee
The proponent of record is Kurt R. Oneto, a partner at the Sacramento election-law firm Nielsen Merksamer, whose firm bio (https://www.nmgovlaw.com/team/kurt-oneto/) says he "has served as counsel and legal strategist to over 60 ballot measure campaigns." The Attorney General's list (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives/active-measures) shows Oneto as proponent of three measures on this ballot: Prop 45 and the two tax measures, Props 41 and 42, that could cancel the billionaire tax. The California Chamber of Commerce says (https://advocacy.calchamber.com/2026/09/11/calchamber-board-of-directors-announces-positions-on-november-ballot-measures/) it "not only strongly supports Proposition 45… but led the effort to qualify the measure"; the Secretary of State's top-funder disclosure (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/top-funders/2000-top-funders-04-01-26.pdf) for the petition drive names a CalChamber-sponsored committee with "major funding from" Building a Better California, Edison International and the California Building Industry Association.
Building a Better California is the committee behind the campaigns against Prop 40 and for Props 41 and 42, the three measures that decide the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/). Its Cal-Access filings show $226.7 million raised between January 1 and September 19, 2026; the FPPC identifies its top donors as Google co-founder Sergey Brin and venture capitalist L. John Doerr III; it has no public website, and its filer telephone number is that of Nielsen Merksamer's San Rafael office. It has given $10 million to the Yes on 45 committee, the largest single contribution on that side.
The FPPC's October 6 list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/) puts the Yes side at $32.8 million from top contributors across three committees: after Building a Better California come the California Building Industry Association's issues committee ($5.65 million, with KB Home and Lennar as its top donors) and the association itself ($2.25 million), a separate CBIA committee funded by homebuilders ($4.1 million), a committee funded by PG&E ($2.4 million), CalChamber ($2 million), Edison International ($2 million), the California Association of Realtors ($1.5 million), a business PAC funded by California Resources Corporation and PG&E ($1.35 million), and $500,000 each from the hospital association, California Resources Corporation and a committee sponsored by Prologis, the logistics real-estate company. The No side reports $22.2 million: Clean and Healthy California, an environmental political committee, $7.08 million; philanthropist Wendy Schmidt, $5 million; the State Building and Construction Trades Council's committees, $2 million; the Laborers, $1.5 million; Operating Engineers Local 12 and the Iron Workers, $1 million and $1.5 million; and the Center for Biological Diversity, Earthjustice and the Natural Resources Defense Council's action fund in smaller amounts.
The lineup is unusual. The construction trades, which generally support building, are against; so are the Laborers, whose members build the projects the measure covers. The No argument's explanation is the measure's labor provisions and its backers: it "was written by the California Chamber of Commerce and financed by gas and electric utilities and corporate PACs." The Yes argument's coalition includes the California Children's Hospital Association, the California Water Association, American Clean Power, LULAC, the NAACP state conference and the California Taxpayers Association.
The arguments: Red tape versus review
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/arguments-rebuttals.htm) is an affordability case: "Permitting delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new home," it says, and Prop 45 "will help lower rents and mortgages." The campaign's own site (https://yesonprop45.com/) adds a commissioned estimate that the measure would raise housing permitting 18.1% and "add nearly 200,000 homes over ten years." It stresses that "Prop. 45 does not exempt a single project from environmental review" and that "cities and counties retain full authority to approve or deny projects."
The No argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/arguments-rebuttals.htm) is a public-health case: Prop 45 "lets projects move forward with far less scrutiny of their harms to air, water and public health," and "reduces public agency requirements to consider public comments." Its campaign site (https://www.noprop45ca.com/) argues the measure "would fast-track polluting projects like data centers, pipelines, and industrial warehouses." Data centers, pipelines and warehouses are not among the nine categories; the measure's definition does include, for every essential project, "all related and ancillary public, private, and utility infrastructure," and whether that clause lets parts of such projects use the track is a reading the campaigns dispute and the text does not settle. The $75,000, 200,000-home and 639-day figures on the Yes side come from a report the campaign commissioned; all of these are claims, printed in the guide with the standard note that arguments "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
Polling and endorsements on Proposition 45
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of 1,103 likely voters, reading the ballot title, found 49% yes, 46% no and 5% undecided, inside the ±3.8-point margin. No other independent poll has published a Prop 45 result. McClatchy's California editorial board, writing for the Sacramento Bee and four other papers, endorsed (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317475362.html) the measure on October 5; the Bakersfield Californian has also endorsed it; the San Francisco Chronicle's editorial board lists its Prop 45 recommendation as "coming soon," and the Los Angeles Times had not published one as of October 12. The parties have split: the California Democratic Party opposes (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 45 and the California Republican Party supports (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it. Governor Newsom, whose campaign released his positions on 12 of the 14 measures on October 9, has not taken one (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/) on Prop 45; he is "still reviewing" it and Prop 41, his spokesperson told the San Francisco Chronicle (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php).
Proposition 45 after November 3: An immediate rewrite of pending reviews, amendable only by two-thirds
If Prop 45 passes, it takes effect on certification and applies "to all pending and future public agency and judicial review and processes for all essential projects," so applicants with reviews under way could withdraw and resubmit under the new chapter, and pending lawsuits would be subject to its litigation rules. The Legislature could adjust it only by a two-thirds vote that "furthers the purposes" of the chapter. If it fails, CEQA continues as the Legislature has been reshaping it since 2025, exemption by exemption. Either way, Proposition 45 is the first time California voters have been asked to decide the shape of environmental review directly, and the question on the ballot is not whether to review essential projects but how long, how deeply, and with what recourse.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, the FPPC contributor list as of October 6, 2026, endorsements as of October 12, 2026, and polling fielded through September 10, 2026.

About (https://igs.berkeley.edu/about)
IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

About (https://igs.berkeley.edu/about)
IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

Voters disengaged and largely unenthusiastic about California’s (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2h95684f)
upcoming gubernatorial primary election. Two Republicans lead the crowded field of Democrats, but none receives more than 17% support. (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2h95684f)

PPIC STATEWIDE SURVEY OCTOBER 2026
Californians and Their GovernmentOctober 2026
Full Crosstabs–Likely Voters Only
Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos KnowledgePanel. Interviews were conducted in
English and Spanish according to the respondents’ preferences. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. Interviewing took place
from October 16—22, 2026.
These crosstabs are based on a subgroup of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error, taking design effects from weighting into consideration, is ±3.8
percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups
is larger. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording,
question order, and survey timing.
If you have any questions or require additional information regarding this survey, please contact surveys@ppic.org

Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos
KnowledgePanel. Interviews were conducted in English and Spanish according to the respondents’
preferences. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. Interviewing took place from October
16—22, 2026.
These crosstabs are based on a subgroup of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error, taking design effects
from weighting into consideration, is ±3.8 percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted
sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups is larger. Sampling
error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as
question wording, question order, and survey timing.

Support slips for Prop 40 and Prop 45
By JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white), BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones) and MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason)

DOWNWARD ARC — Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects. Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure. But Prop 45 also plunged underwater. Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots. Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers. Opponents of the wealth tax have argued it could eventually be expanded to hit working Californians. Supporters disputed both claims.
PROP 3 HOLDS — The wealth tax’s slide in the polls hasn’t extended to Proposition 3, which would make permanent an existing tax on top earners to fund education. Support for that measure held steady at 58%, a result that may ease union proponents’ fears that opposition to Proposition 40 could spill over to Prop 3.
Those divergent trendlines reflected starkly different political and financial realities. The Prop 3 campaign has raised more than $80 million and faced no funded opposition; the wealth tax effort has operated on a shoestring budget as billionaires spend hundreds of millions of dollars against it. Democrats are largely unified behind Prop 3, while Prop 40 has been extraordinarily divisive within the party.
Prop 40 was not the only SEIU-UHW-championed measure to backslide as opponents piled on. Support for Proposition 44, which would regulate clinics, shrank to just 25% in the face of a $44 million health care industry counteroffensive. In both cases, SEIU-UHW spent millions on qualification but has not followed up with a comparable advertising campaign.
Two billionaire-funded measures designed to torpedo Prop 40 were also on the bubble amid tightening polling: Proposition 41 declined from a 51-44 majority in September to 48-49 this month, and Proposition 42 went from 54-43 to 51-47. Wealthy backers have largely focused on 42, pouring some $65 million into the campaign this month. But the rest of the ballot is looking increasingly predictable as campaigns either held steady or saw polling gaps expand.
THE REST OF THE BALLOT — Voters broadly support two housing bonds (Proposition 1 and Proposition 37), an expansion of the state’s “rainy day” reserve fund (Proposition 2), and an immunology research bond (Proposition 38). A voter ID measure (Proposition 39) and an initiative making it harder to raise local taxes (Proposition 43) are both trailing by double-digit margins. And two measures to institute public election financing (Proposition 4) and overhaul recalls (Proposition 5) remain below majority support despite creeping up to 45%.
