DOWNWARD ARC — Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects. Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure. But Prop 45 also plunged underwater. Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots. Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers. Opponents of the wealth tax have argued it could eventually be expanded to hit working Californians. Supporters disputed both claims.
PROP 3 HOLDS — The wealth tax’s slide in the polls hasn’t extended to Proposition 3, which would make permanent an existing tax on top earners to fund education. Support for that measure held steady at 58%, a result that may ease union proponents’ fears that opposition to Proposition 40 could spill over to Prop 3.
Those divergent trendlines reflected starkly different political and financial realities. The Prop 3 campaign has raised more than $80 million and faced no funded opposition; the wealth tax effort has operated on a shoestring budget as billionaires spend hundreds of millions of dollars against it. Democrats are largely unified behind Prop 3, while Prop 40 has been extraordinarily divisive within the party.
Prop 40 was not the only SEIU-UHW-championed measure to backslide as opponents piled on. Support for Proposition 44, which would regulate clinics, shrank to just 25% in the face of a $44 million health care industry counteroffensive. In both cases, SEIU-UHW spent millions on qualification but has not followed up with a comparable advertising campaign.
Two billionaire-funded measures designed to torpedo Prop 40 were also on the bubble amid tightening polling: Proposition 41 declined from a 51-44 majority in September to 48-49 this month, and Proposition 42 went from 54-43 to 51-47. Wealthy backers have largely focused on 42, pouring some $65 million into the campaign this month. But the rest of the ballot is looking increasingly predictable as campaigns either held steady or saw polling gaps expand.
THE REST OF THE BALLOT — Voters broadly support two housing bonds (Proposition 1 and Proposition 37), an expansion of the state’s “rainy day” reserve fund (Proposition 2), and an immunology research bond (Proposition 38). A voter ID measure (Proposition 39) and an initiative making it harder to raise local taxes (Proposition 43) are both trailing by double-digit margins. And two measures to institute public election financing (Proposition 4) and overhaul recalls (Proposition 5) remain below majority support despite creeping up to 45%.
GOOD MORNING. Happy Wednesday. Thanks for waking up with California Playbook.
Like what you’re reading? Sign up (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/californiaplaybook) to get California Playbook in your inbox, and forward it to a friend. Have a tip for Playbook? Drop us a line at [email protected] (https://www.politico.com/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#acc1c1cddfc3c2ecdcc3c0c5d8c5cfc382cfc3c1) and [email protected] (https://www.politico.com/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#2a484045444f596a5a4546435e43494504494547), or on X — @melmason (https://x.com/melmason) and @jonesblakej (https://x.com/jonesblakej). Or you can text us at ‪ 916-562-0685 ‬‪ — save it as “ CA Playbook ” in your contacts.
WHO WON THE DAY? Prop 40 opponents , who received good news in the PPIC poll.
WHERE’S GAVIN? In Los Angeles, having a fireside chat with California Science Center CEO Jeffrey Rudolph during a media preview of the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center.
TOP READS
SHATTERED RECORDS — Billionaire opponents of California’s proposed wealth tax have spent more fighting it than they ever have on a political cause in the state, according to a POLITICO analysis.
A record $612 million from more than 70 current and former California billionaires is flooding this year’s state elections , nearly half of it to groups working to defeat the wealth tax initiative on Tuesday’s ballot, POLITICO found.
The fight over Prop 40 has brought California’s wealthiest residents — many from its native tech industry — together in an unprecedented show of political coordination, the new data reveals. Tech leaders say the wealth tax has accelerated plans for broader political engagement this cycle, building networks that could be the foundation for future campaigns.
Read the full story from Christine Mui and Sean McMinn here (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/28/billionaires-spending-california-wealth-tax-01137778) .
IN THE COURTS
In this Aug. 30, 2021, file photo, mail-in ballots run through a sorting machine at the Sacramento County Registrar of Voters office in Sacramento, California. | Rich Pedroncelli/AP
ELECTION CLAIM SKEPTIC — A federal judge in California signaled Tuesday that he is preparing to reject the Trump administration’s emergency effort to force the state to set aside and review any votes cast by people on a list of 20,000 registered voters the Department of Homeland Security has identified as likely noncitizens.
After a three-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge David Carter instead said he needed a far more extensive briefing on the matter that would extend well past Election Day. In effect, it’s a defeat for the Justice Department, which had demanded the judge immediately force the state to comply. Carter, a Clinton appointee, said DOJ could prosecute anyone it identifies as casting an illegal ballot.
“Of course no one wants a noncitizen voting. Anybody taking that position, it’s a ridiculous position,” he said.
The judge concluded with a stark warning for DOJ, however, after state officials complained that the Trump administration had made menacing comments about potentially prosecuting election workers who tabulated the votes of noncitizens: “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately.”
Carter said he would issue a formal order Wednesday. — Kyle Cheney
First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli speaks during an announcement at Department of Justice headquarters in Washington on Nov. 19, 2025. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
WHAT’S IN A NAME — A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Bill Essayli is unlawfully acting as a “de facto” U.S. attorney.
Judge J. Michael Seabright , who last year ruled that Essayli was illegally serving in the role (https://www.politico.com/news/2025/10/28/judge-los-angeles-top-federal-prosecutor-illegally-appointed-00626804) of acting U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote that “Essayli—even in his designated role as a Special Attorney and FAUSA—is disqualified from (1) participating in or supervising these cases, or (2) otherwise supervising any attorneys in the handling of these cases.”
Essayli said in a statement that he respectfully disagreed with the ruling.
“The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department,” he said.
Essayli added that the motion was automatically stayed, and that the status quo will likely remain while the DOJ appeals the decision. “Ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court,” he said, “and I look forward to serving in my current role until then.” — Nicole Norman
ELECTION YEAR
Chad Bianco speaks during a California gubernatorial debate hosted by CBS Bay Area and the San Francisco Examiner in San Francisco, Thursday, May 14, 2026. | Godofredo A. Vásquez/AP
RELUCTANT SUPPORT? — It was hardly a ringing endorsement, but Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco , who previously declined to endorse (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) Steve Hilton in the governor’s race after losing the primary, voiced support for his fellow Republican’s candidacy on Tuesday.
“I don’t care if you like him or not. We absolutely need Steve Hilton to win this race for governor,” Bianco said in a video on social media (https://x.com/ChadBianco/status/2115188593425850374?a=NXWO74gQaasvSVU-EC4&s=20).
Bianco in May argued (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) that President Donald Trump ’s endorsement of Hilton (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/04/06/before-trump-backed-hilton-loomer-was-already-at-work-00861205) would hurt the former Fox News host in California. But he urged followers to vote for Hilton in the video, anyway, saying “we need balance” amid Democratic rule.
IN THE PHONE BANK — Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas rallied volunteers at a phone bank supporting Democrat Amy Slavensky , telling them her incumbent opponent Assemblymember Josh Hoover is a “nice guy, but he doesn’t represent this community’s interests.” Outgoing Women’s Caucus Chair Cecilia Aguiar-Curry said electing Slavensky, a former school administrator, was a priority of the caucus. And Assemblymember Gail Pellerin , a former local elections official, instructed callers to encourage voters to drop off their ballots in person rather than by mail, citing concerns about possible Trump administration interference.
“We cannot rely on the United States Postal Service right now because they are under the control of this Trump administration, and we don’t want those ballots to get held somewhere and not in the hands of the elections official,” Pellerin told the volunteers gathered in the Sacramento suburb of Fair Oaks.
The event’s attendance by several Democratic officials, including Assemblymember Patrick Ahrens , underscored the force with which their party is trying to oust Hoover despite his moderate profile and, as Rivas seemed to acknowledge, affable demeanor. The state Democratic Party has poured more than $2 million into defeating the frontline Republican, one of several incumbents it’s trying to oust after losing seats in both chambers of the Legislature last cycle.
Super PACs, including the GOP caucus-aligned Legislative Action Victory PAC and another sponsored by CalChamber, have collectively spent more than $3 million defending Hoover and blasting Slavensky.
LOS ANGELES
Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman speaks during a campaign event on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, in Sylmar, California. | William Liang/AP
POWER PLAY — Frustration over sky-high electricity bills is becoming a flashpoint in the closing days of the Los Angeles mayor’s race, with Karen Bass and her progressive challenger, Nithya Raman , trading blows over utility costs that have soared amid record-breaking heatwaves, Alex Nieves reports for subscribers (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/10/the-la-mayors-race-goes-electric-01137758).
The fracas began early last week after Raman held a press conference alongside frustrated Los Angeles Department of Water and Power customers, where the council member blamed Bass for letting the utility raise electricity and water rates without City Council approval — and promised to audit the department. Bass has responded with promises to lower bills and investigate the city’s climbing utility costs.
The last-minute brawl comes as candidates statewide contend with high electricity prices and broader concerns about the cost of living — an issue (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) which is among voters’ top concerns. California’s electricity rates are the second-highest in the U.S., behind only Hawaii. Read last night’s California Currents (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-currents/2026/10/27/ramans-electric-closing-message-01137445) to see how both campaigns are trying to navigate energy affordability angst ahead of Election Day.

UCLA SUIT — For the second time this month, the University of California has asked a federal judge to dismiss a lawsuit by the Department of Justice alleging that UCLA failed to properly address antisemitic incidents during protests over Israel’s war against Hamas.

PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
CON
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.

OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for specified project categories (including most housing, transportation, water, health, wildfire mitigation, educational facility, internet access, and clean energy projects). For these types of projects, this measure:
Sets deadlines for public agencies to complete environmental review and take required actions.
Allows expedited review of environmental impacts, limiting public agencies’ current obligation to consider a range of feasible project alternatives to reduce environmental impacts.
Establishes deadlines for filing and resolving lawsuits challenging project approvals; limits evidence courts may consider and relief courts can order.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars annually—potentially exceeding $100 million annually—to implement new project review and court challenge procedures for eligible projects. Fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits would partly cover these costs.
In the longer term, uncertain, but potentially more significant positive or negative fiscal effects for state and local governments. The overall effect depends, in part, on how the new procedures change the number of eligible projects that get built and whether those projects have different environmental impacts.

PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
State Law Requires Government Agencies to Review the Environmental Impacts of Proposed Projects. State and local government agencies are responsible for reviewing and approving certain projects before they can be built. As part of this process, the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires an agency to consider how a project might negatively affect the environment before approving it. CEQA applies to many types of public and private projects, such as housing developments, school facilities, and highway expansions. Some exceptions apply. For example, state law exempts certain housing developments located near public transit from needing a CEQA review.
How the CEQA Process Works. The government agency first determines if CEQA applies to a project. If so, it then determines if the project could significantly affect the environment and if those impacts could be avoided or reduced with minor changes to the project. If making minor changes cannot avoid or reduce significant impacts, the agency must do a more detailed review called an environmental impact report (EIR). (The majority of projects do not require an EIR; however, EIRs are somewhat more common for large and complex projects.) The EIR analyzes possible environmental impacts the project could cause and considers alternatives that could reduce those impacts. After finishing the environmental review, the agency decides whether to approve the project. At certain times during this process, the government agency must seek and consider comments about the project’s environmental review from the public and other government agencies.
People Can Sue the Government Agency About Its CEQA Review. After a government agency has completed the CEQA review and decided whether to approve a project, people who think the agency did not follow the CEQA process correctly can sue the agency. For example, a project opponent might argue that the environmental analysis was inadequate. If the court finds that the agency did not follow CEQA correctly, it can stop the whole project and require the agency to fix the part of the process that was problematic.
Many Projects Also Need to Get Other Approvals. Besides CEQA review, many projects need approval or permits from other local and/or state government agencies before they can proceed. For example, a business that wants to build a health clinic might need the local government to change land use rules before it can proceed. It also may need state agencies to review and approve how the project might affect certain wildlife species and water quality.
PROPOSAL
Proposition 45 creates new procedures for reviewing certain types of projects that it defines as “essential.” Figure 1 lists the types of projects eligible for the new procedures. The proposition (1) tightens time limits for CEQA review, permits, and court challenges; (2) changes parts of the CEQA review process; and (3) changes the court’s review process for CEQA lawsuits. The proposition gives eligible project applicants the option of using the new procedures or existing procedures.
Tightens Time Limits for Review and Court Challenges of Eligible Projects. Proposition 45 creates more binding time limits for state and local governments to do both CEQA and permitting reviews. This includes time limits for determining if a project application is complete, finishing the EIR, and granting other types of approvals and permits. For example, Proposition 45 allows an applicant to request an agency hearing- and potentially file a lawsuit with the courts-if an agency does not meet the 365-business-day time limit for finishing the EIR. The proposition also creates a time limit for courts to resolve legal challenges.
Changes CEQA Review for Eligible Projects. For eligible projects, Proposition 45 makes several changes to the CEQA review process, including:
Application Process. Requires the government agency to specify all information that must be included in an application before it is submitted. (Current law allows agencies to repeatedly request additional information or project changes.)
How Environmental Impacts Are Assessed. Requires the agency to assess potential environmental impacts based on the laws and standards in place at the time the project application is submitted. (Current law lets the agency consider new information and revise its review standards when doing the EIR.)
Project Alternatives. Allows the applicant to develop only one project alternative for the agency to consider. (Current law requires the agency-not the applicant-to develop and consider multiple project alternatives that could reduce environmental impacts.)
Consultation With Native Tribes. Requires the agency and applicant to consult about the project only with California native tribes that have been formally recognized by the federal government. (Current law requires consultation with a wider range of tribes.)
Public Comment Periods. Limits how long the agency can accept comments from the public and other government agencies about the project. (Current law sets a minimum number of days-not a maximum-for public review.)
Changes How Courts Review Challenges to Eligible Projects. Proposition 45 makes several changes to the court’s review process when someone challenges a government agency’s approval of an eligible project. For example, it reduces the scope of what the court can consider in CEQA lawsuits. The proposition also prevents the court from stopping the whole project if it finds that the agency did not follow CEQA correctly. Instead, the court can only stop the part of the project where the environmental review did not comply with CEQA while the agency fixes the problem.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Initial Costs for State and Local Governments. During the first several years, Proposition 45 likely would increase costs for the state and local governments, including state courts. These costs likely would be in the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially exceeding $100 million annually . For example, state and local governments would have costs to develop new guidelines and standards for reviewing eligible projects’ environmental impacts, meet tighter time limits, and address court challenges. Fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits would cover some of these costs. After this initial period, while some costs could continue, others likely would decline over time. For example, the changes to how courts can review CEQA lawsuits could mean fewer people will sue in the future, which could reduce costs for agencies and state courts in the long term.
In the Longer Term, Uncertain but Potentially More Significant Fiscal Effects. Proposition 45’s changes to project review and court challenge procedures for eligible projects could have various fiscal effects for state and local governments. The overall fiscal effect of these changes-positive or negative-is uncertain but could be more substantial than the near-term effects. For example, two effects that could have significant but uncertain impacts are:
More Projects and Faster Timing. To the degree that Proposition 45’s changes to project review and court challenge procedures lead to eligible public projects being constructed more quickly, state and local governments likely would have lower project costs. Additionally, if the proposition’s changes result in more projects being completed overall, it could lead to an increase in tax revenues, such as from property taxes.
Negative Environmental Impacts. To the degree that Proposition 45’s changes to project review and court challenge procedures lead to approval of projects with negative environmental impacts that would not have otherwise occurred, government agencies could face higher costs to respond to those impacts.

PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 45
LENGTHY DELAYS AND RED TAPE ARE BLOCKING ESSENTIAL PROJECTS & DRIVING UP OUR COST OF LIVING.
Families cannot afford to live in California because we are failing to deliver the basics. California’s outdated system for approving essential housing, water, clean energy, roads, schools, hospitals, and wildfire prevention projects is too slow, too bureaucratic, and too costly—driving up the cost of living for everyone.
Endless delays, red tape, and frivolous lawsuits make life more expensive and block the projects Californians need—driving up costs for housing, electricity, and water; wasting taxpayer dollars; worsening wildfire risk; increasing traffic; overcrowding schools; and delaying hospital and infrastructure upgrades.
PROP. 45 LOWERS OUR HIGH COST OF LIVING BY MAKING IT FASTER & LESS EXPENSIVE TO BUILD ESSENTIAL PROJECTS.
Prop. 45 streamlines approvals by setting enforceable timelines for project approvals; requires courts and government agencies to base decisions on the laws and regulations in place when the project application is submitted; and creates a faster, more predictable process for legal challenges while reducing frivolous lawsuits.
PROP. 45 STREAMLINES CALIFORNIA’S MOST-PRESSING ESSENTIAL PROJECTS, INCLUDING:
• Water quality and supply projects • Hospitals and healthcare facilities • Housing, including homes and apartments • Wildfire prevention • Schools and classrooms • Roads, bridges and transit • Clean energy and electric grid reliability infrastructure
PROP. 45 WILL:
REDUCE THE COST OF HOUSING. Permitting delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new home. Prop. 45 will help lower rents and mortgages and save families tens of thousands of dollars on a home purchase.
LOWER ELECTRICITY COSTS. Delays in building clean energy and electric grid infrastructure drive up electricity costs for working families. Prop. 45 helps lower electricity costs.
PROTECT TAXPAYERS. Lengthy delays drive massive cost overruns on public projects—roads, schools, hospitals, water systems, and wildfire prevention—costing taxpayers billions more. Prop. 45 cuts costly delays, reduces costs, and helps keep projects on time and on budget.
CREATE GOOD-PAYING JOBS AND STRENGTHEN OUR ECONOMY. Prop. 45 will create tens of thousands of good-paying jobs and billions in economic activity.
PROP. 45 MAINTAINS CALIFORNIA’S STRONGEST-IN-THE-NATION ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTIONS.
California should not have to choose between protecting the environment and building the essential projects we need. Under Prop. 45, projects must comply with all of California strong environmental laws protecting our air, water, wildlife, and health. Prop. 45 does not exempt a single project from environmental review.
PROP. 45 PROTECTS COMMUNITY INPUT AND LOCAL DECISION MAKING.
Under Prop. 45, cities and counties retain full authority to approve or deny projects, and residents keep a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their communities.
AFFORDABLE HOUSING ADVOCATES, HEALTHCARE PROFESSIONALS, EDUCATORS, WATER PROVIDERS, CLEAN ENERGY LEADERS AND CIVIL RIGHTS LEADERS SUPPORT PROP. 45.
Prop. 45 is supported by a broad coalition of organizations, including:
• American Clean Power—California • California League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC) • NAACP California/Hawaii State Conference • California Taxpayers Association • Environmental Policy Innovation Center
YES ON PROP. 45 TO BUILD A MORE AFFORDABLE CALIFORNIA.
Every year of delay means Californians wait longer and pay more for the essential projects we need. It’s time to cut red tape, protect our environment and build the projects California needs to make life more affordable.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 45.
YESonProp45.com
Ann-Louise Kuhns , President
California Children’s Hospital Association
Jennifer Capitolo , Executive Director
California Water Association
Jenna Abbott , Executive Director
California Council on Affordable Housing
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 45
PROPOSITION 45 WON’T LOWER YOUR COSTS.
It doesn’t require a single project to lower your rent, your mortgage, or your utility bills. 45’s corporate funders profit while you bear the cost of their pollution.
PROP. 45 DOESN’T DELIVER AN AFFORDABLE CALIFORNIA. IT LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW AND RISKS PUBLIC HEALTH.
Prop. 45 could have been about building what California needs. It isn’t. Funded by gas and electric utilities and corporate PACs, Prop. 45 cuts their costs, not yours. Prop. 45 flips California law to protect their projects, harming public health and our air and water.
PROP. 45 PUTS YOUR HEALTH AT RISK AND STICKS YOU WITH THE BILL. Weaker environmental review means more pollution near homes and schools, more asthma and more emergency-room visits. When polluters don’t clean up, taxpayers and ratepayers pay more to cover the costs.
PROP. 45 TAKES AWAY PUBLIC INPUT. It limits the environmental review of new projects and your right to provide input and be heard. 45 even gives developers new rights to challenge cities and counties, while making it more difficult for project opponents to successfully challenge an agency’s decision.
Prop. 45 rewrites the rules that govern how California protects its citizens from the harm caused by major developments. Prop. 45 weakens environmental safeguards and radically shifts power to corporate polluters.
Protect your air quality, your drinking water, your family’s health, your tax dollars, and your right to be heard.
Join nurses, community and public health advocates.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 45.
www.NoProp45CA.com
Chris Tarver , R.N., President
American Nurses Association, CA
Vanessa Forsythe , RN
California Nurses for Environmental Health and Justice
Martha Arguello , Executive Director
Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 45
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. VOTE NO ON PROP. 45 TO PROTECT WATER, AIR QUALITY AND PUBLIC HEALTH.
Proposition 45 limits both the environmental review of major new development projects and the public’s right to be heard. Prop. 45 lets projects move forward with far less scrutiny of their harms to air, water and public health.
PROP. 45 WEAKENS CRITICAL PROTECTIONS FOR AIR AND WATER QUALITY BY GUTTING THE CALIFORNIA ENVIRONMENTAL QUALITY ACT (CEQA).
CEQA is California’s most important air and water quality protection law. It requires public agencies to identify, publicly disclose, and consider reducing harm to air, water, and wildlife before approving projects. Prop. 45 eliminates many of CEQA’s existing protections— letting developers fast-track the polluting projects you don’t want next door, with fewer protections for the water you drink and air you breathe.
PROP. 45 CUTS THE PUBLIC OUT OF DECISIONS THAT AFFECT YOUR FAMILY.
Today, you have a voice in what’s built near you and your family. Prop. 45 reduces public agency requirements to consider public comments on proposed projects—comments that often expose potential contamination of air and water, and damage to our coast, rivers, and wildlife. If Prop. 45 passes, decisions about what gets built near your home, your children’s school, and your water supply would be made with less information and less public input. Prop. 45 reduces your ability to protect your family and community from harm.
We need CEQA’s protections more than ever since federal protections have been weakened.
THEY POLLUTE. YOU PAY.
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office warns Prop. 45 could approve projects that result in “unintended negative environmental impacts.” When corporations aren’t required to reduce their pollution, taxpayers get stuck paying to clean up cancer-causing chemicals from our drinking water and contaminated lands.
PROP. 45 WON’T LOWER YOUR COSTS.
Prop. 45 doesn’t include any requirement to lower your housing costs or your utility bills. The corporations paying for Prop. 45 will profit while you keep paying.
WHO’S BEHIND PROP. 45?
Prop. 45 was written by the California Chamber of Commerce and financed by gas and electric utilities and corporate PACs. It gives the polluters and corporations funding Prop. 45 greater freedom to put whatever they want next to your home. Your family’s health and environmental quality are more important than corporate profits.
JOIN A BROAD COALITION OF PUBLIC HEALTH, ENVIRONMENTAL, AND COMMUNITY GROUPS OPPOSING PROP. 45, INCLUDING:
• National Wildlife Federation • California Communities Against Toxics • California Environmental Voters • California Environmental Justice Alliance • California Nurses for Environmental Health & Justice • Clean Water Action • Coalition for Clean Air • Physicians for Social Responsibility—Los Angeles
Whether you’re a Democrat, a Republican, or an independent, vote NO on Prop. 45 to protect your air and water, your tax dollars, and your right to be heard.
VOTE NO on Prop. 45.
www.NoProp45CA.com .
Joe Lyou , President
Coalition for Clean Air
Jennifer Clary , California Director
Clean Water Action
Matt Abularach-Macias , Political Director
California Environmental Voters
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 45
PROP. 45 IS THE CHANGE WE NEED TO BUILD A MORE AFFORDABLE CALIFORNIA.
The status quo is failing California. Families cannot afford to live here because we’re failing to deliver the basics. Endless delays, lawsuits and red tape are driving up the cost of essentials—housing, water, electricity, schools, roads, healthcare and wildfire protection.
We have a choice: accept the failing status quo—or fix it. PROP. 45 FIXES OUR BROKEN PROJECT APPROVAL SYSTEM by eliminating unnecessary delays for essential projects—lowering our cost of living and improving our quality of life.
PROP. 45’s OPPONENTS ARE MISLEADING VOTERS TO PROTECT THE BROKEN STATUS QUO.
The same opponents fighting Prop. 45 have spent decades using these same scare tactics to block even modest reforms. They’re fighting to preserve the broken status quo that’s making California unaffordable and lowering our quality of life.
WE DON’T HAVE TO CHOOSE BETWEEN PROTECTING THE ENVIRONMENT AND BUILDING ESSENTIAL PROJECTS.
FACT: Prop. 45 maintains every federal, state and local environmental law protecting our air, water, wildlife, and public health, including the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act.
FACT: Prop. 45 does not eliminate a single environmental law or exempt a single project from environmental review.
FACT: Communities keep their voice. Residents maintain their right to provide public comments, oppose projects, and sue to stop projects.
FACT: Prop. 45 only applies to essential projects : water, hospitals, housing, schools, roads, transit, clean energy, and wildfire prevention.
THE CHOICE IS SIMPLE: accept the broken status quo—or fix it.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 45 TO BUILD A MORE AFFORDABLE CALIFORNIA.
Ann-Louise Kuhns , President
California Children’s Hospital Association
Ruben Grijalva , Former California State Fire Marshal
CAL FIRE
Robert Rivinius , President
Family Business Association of California

# Proposition 45 Would Establish New CEQA Rules for Essential Projects
Prop 45, titled the “Building an Affordable California Act,” is a ballot initiative that, if approved by voters, would establish new deadlines for environmental review, narrow the scope of CEQA litigation, and limit the remedies available to courts for certain “essential projects,” including certain housing projects, clean energy projects, education facilities, and more.
Under Prop 45, streamlined review and approval of such projects would be declared a matter of statewide concern, and the state would occupy the field in this area.
The measure’s stated purposes include making California more affordable by streamlining and speeding approval of essential projects while maintaining environmental protections.
If a majority of voters approve Prop 45, it would take effect within weeks of the election (specifically, on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote) and would reach not only new applications but also agency proceedings and lawsuits already underway.
Prop 45 would not exempt essential projects from environmental review at either the state or local level, nor reduce an agency’s authority to approve or disapprove them.
Use of the new procedures generally would be voluntary: applicants could elect to use none, some, or all of the measure’s provisions, subject to certain mandatory tribal consultation and labor requirements for projects that utilize the chapter.

## How would Proposition 45 change CEQA?
Proposition 45, the Building an Affordable California Act, is a statewide initiative on California’s November 3, 2026 ballot.
The measure would amend CEQA, the state’s landmark environmental law, by establishing new environmental review and judicial procedures that applicants could elect to use for qualifying projects.
The measure defines these as “essential projects” across eight categories: housing, water, clean energy, public health, public safety, broadband, education and transportation.
Ancillary infrastructure required to serve an essential project may also qualify.
Certain projects are specifically excluded, including California High-Speed Rail, the Delta Conveyance Project, detention facilities and new oil or natural gas production facilities.
For qualifying projects using the new procedures, key provisions include:
**Review timelines:** Agencies would generally have 30 days to determine whether an application is complete and another 30 days to determine the type of environmental review required.

## California voters will decide whether Prop 45 should create faster environmental review and court-challenge procedures for certain public and private projects.

In November, California voters will decide on **Proposition (Prop) 45**, also known as the “Building an Affordable California Act" or the Expedited Environmental Review Process for Certain Projects Initiative.
If approved, the initiative would change the environmental review process established under the **California Environmental Quality Act**, or CEQA.
Enacted in 1970, CEQA requires state and local agencies to identify and disclose the potential environmental effects of projects they propose to carry out, fund or approve.
Agencies must also consider feasible alternatives and measures to avoid or reduce significant environmental harm.
...

To accelerate the process, lead agencies would be required to issue permit decisions when environmental reviews are completed instead of afterward.
If an agency missed a deadline, the applicant could grant additional time or request a final agency hearing.
The measure would also allow applicants to challenge adverse agency decisions in court and require those cases to be resolved within 270 days.

Proposition 45: Environmental Review
Proposition 45: Environmental Review
Proposition 45: Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
Building an Affordable California Act
Summary
Proposition 45 began asinitiative 25-0023 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf), filed by proponent Kurt Oneto with the California Attorney General’s Office on October 21, 2025. The initiative was cleared for signature gathering on December 26, 2025. Supporters submitted signatures in April 2026 and the Secretary of State reported that the minimum signature requirement had been met in June 2026. The measure therefore qualified for the November 2026 ballot.
Proposition 45 creates a new review process for certain projects defined as “essential.” The measure sets stricter deadlines for state and local agencies to complete both CEQA and permitting reviews. It also establishes new deadlines for issuing permits and resolving court challenges. Eligible applicants could choose these new procedures instead of the existing process.
The process for California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) reviews is changed for eligible projects. Specifically, government agencies must specify all information that an application must contain before it is submitted, limiting their ability to request additional information or project changes later. Environmental impacts generally would be assessed using laws and standards in place when the application was submitted, rather than allowing agencies to revise review standards based on later changes. Applicants could develop a single project alternative rather than having the agency develop and consider multiple alternatives. The measure also limits tribal consultation to federally recognized California tribes and places maximum time limits on comments from the public and other government agencies regarding the project.
The measure also changes the guidelines and process for CEQA lawsuits. When someone challenges a government agency’s approval of an eligible project, courts would be limited in what they could consider when determining whether the agency complied with CEQA. Courts generally could not halt the entire project if they found a CEQA violation. Instead, a court could halt only the portion of the project affected by the violation while the agency corrects the problem, allowing other parts of the project to proceed.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 45 would initially increase state and local government costs, including state court costs, by tens of millions of dollars annually and potentially more than $100 million per year. These costs would result from developing new environmental review guidelines, meeting tighter deadlines, and handling legal challenges. Some costs would be covered by fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits and could potentially reduce over time.
The measure’s longer-term fiscal effects are uncertain and could be more significant. Changes to review and court challenge rules could lead to projects being completed more quickly. In these cases, state and local governments would likely have lower project costs. If more projects are completed, there could be an increase in tax revenues. However, governments could also face higher costs if projects approved under the new procedures result in negative environmental impacts that require a government response.
What your vote means
YES: Supports creating new review procedures for certain projects defined as “essential,” including stricter deadlines for environmental reviews and permits, changes to how project alternatives and environmental impacts are considered, and limits on the timing, scope, and remedies of CEQA lawsuits.
NO: Opposes these changes and keeps the existing CEQA review and court challenge procedures for these projects, including current requirements for considering project alternatives and existing rules governing environmental review timelines and CEQA lawsuits.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that current rules around projects are too bureaucratic and expensive. They claim that Proposition 45 would reduce delays and costs associated with approving essential projects, including housing, water, clean energy, transportation, schools, hospitals, and wildfire prevention projects. They claim tighter approval timelines and a faster process for CEQA lawsuits would lower project costs, protect taxpayers, and create jobs. Supporters also maintain that projects would remain subject to California’s environmental laws, local approval, and public input.
Opponents argue that Proposition 45 would weaken environmental review and reduce public input on major development projects. They contend that placing limits on CEQA reviews, public comment periods, and court challenges could allow projects to move forward without the necessary review of possible impacts on air, water, public health, and wildlife, potentially leaving taxpayers responsible for addressing environmental damage. Opponents also argue that the measure contains no requirement that faster project approvals result in lower housing or utility costs.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). California CEQA reform on the ballot: Understanding Prop 45's fast track for "essential projects"
Proposition 45 would let housing, water, clean-energy, hospital, school, broadband, wildfire and transportation projects opt into a new CEQA track with binding deadlines, fewer alternatives and narrower lawsuits. The changes, the 2025 baseline, the funders and the cost.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 12, 2026

California CEQA reform through Proposition 45 would change the approval process for housing, water, energy and infrastructure projects from November 2026.
Proposition 45 would add a new chapter to the California Environmental Quality Act, the 1970 law that requires public agencies to study and disclose a project's environmental effects before approving it. The chapter, titled the "Building an Affordable California Act," applies to nine categories of projects the measure calls essential: housing, water systems, clean energy, medical facilities, fire and police stations, wildfire risk reduction, broadband, education facilities and transportation. For those projects, and only if the applicant chooses, it replaces CEQA's open-ended timelines with fixed ones, narrows what an environmental review must consider, caps public comment, and restricts what a court can do when a review is challenged. It is a statute, placed on the ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/) by petition, and it is the closest contest among the 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/): 49% yes to 46% no in PPIC's September survey.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California’s November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure’s rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The measure's own framing is affordability: "California's outdated system for approving essential projects is too slow, too bureaucratic, and too costly," its findings begin. Its opponents' framing is pollution: the measure "lets projects move forward with far less scrutiny of their harms to air, water and public health." Both sides agree on one thing the Legislative Analyst's Office also states: Prop 45 "does not exempt any essential project from environmental review." What it changes is the process. This explainer sets out that process as the text defines it, what the Legislature already changed in 2025, what the LAO says it would cost, and who is paying.
Proposition 45 creates an opt-in CEQA track for nine project categories
The text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds sections 21010 through 21034 to the Public Resources Code. Section 21015 makes the track voluntary: an applicant "may elect to utilize none, some, or all of the provisions of this chapter," in combination with or instead of other laws, and nothing "requires an applicant seeking approval of a project that meets the definition of an essential project to utilize this chapter." Section 21014 makes it binding on government: the chapter "shall apply to all public agencies," and "to the extent a conflict exists between this chapter and any other law, this chapter shall control." It also preserves existing exemptions and lets applicants with pending applications withdraw and resubmit under the new rules.
The nine categories are defined in section 21028, with exclusions written into each. Housing includes residential, mixed-use developments that are at least two-thirds residential, shelters, farmworker and student housing, and commercial-to-residential conversions. Water projects exclude "Delta conveyance facilities." Clean energy includes solar, wind, geothermal, small hydro, non-fossil hydrogen, microgrids, carbon capture and storage, and transmission, but "excludes producing or generating electricity from nuclear power." Public safety covers fire, police and sheriff's stations, "excluding any portion used as a jail or other detention facility," plus wildfire risk reduction such as undergrounding lines, fuel breaks and home hardening. Transportation covers roads, highways and transit under Article XIX of the Constitution and electric-vehicle charging, but "does not include a high-speed train." Medical facilities, broadband and education facilities, including those of UC, CSU, community colleges, school districts, charter schools and nonprofit private colleges, round out the list. An essential project "does not include a jail or other detention facility, or involve the development of a new oil or natural gas production facility," and each category carries "all related and ancillary public, private, and utility infrastructure."
CEQA today, and the changes the Legislature made in 2025

When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).
