Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). The Legislature has already carved large holes in that process. In June 2025, as part of the budget, Governor Newsom signed (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2025/06/30/governor-newsom-signs-into-law-groundbreaking-reforms-to-build-more-housing-affordability/) AB 130 and SB 131. AB 130 exempts from CEQA entirely infill housing on sites of up to 20 acres in cities or urban areas that are consistent with local zoning. SB 131 exempts day care centers, federally qualified health centers, food banks, advanced manufacturing facilities, wildfire risk-reduction projects, broadband in local rights of way, certain water projects and housing-element rezonings, and creates a "near-miss" rule under which a project that fails an exemption on a single condition is reviewed only for the effects of that condition. The Governor continued in September 2026, signing CEQA bills for fire stations (AB 2152), hospitals (AB 2231), day care zoning (SB 299), geothermal exploration (AB 2234) and an urban rail station (SB 1375), while vetoing (https://www.gov.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Veto-Message-SB-954.pdf) SB 954, which would have narrowed the advanced-manufacturing exemption: the exemption "should be given a meaningful opportunity to work," he wrote.
Prop 45 is different in kind. The 2025 laws exempt specific project types from CEQA; Prop 45 exempts nothing but rewrites the procedure for everything in its nine categories, regardless of size, from a four-unit infill lot to a transmission line, and it does so by initiative, which the Legislature can amend only by a two-thirds vote "consistent with, and furthers the purposes of, this chapter," after the bill has been in print for 12 business days. Prop 45 also incorporates AB 130's labor rule, applying prevailing-wage requirements to housing "solely to buildings over 85 feet in height."
Proposition 45 is replacing CEQA's open-ended review and litigation timelines with fixed clocks and narrower court remedies for nine categories of essential projects, as the measure's text and the Legislative Analyst's Office describe in October 2026. The clocks: 30 days to accept an application, 365 business days to decide an EIR
The measure's first mechanism is deadlines with consequences. Under section 21017, an agency has 30 days to tell an applicant whether an application is complete, with "an exhaustive written corrections list"; if it misses the deadline, "the initial application shall be deemed complete." An application cannot be rejected for lacking studies that were not on a published checklist, and the agency "shall not request or require an applicant to provide any new information unless that information was included on the exhaustive written corrections list."
Sections 21018 and 21019 then set the review clock: a final decision on an environmental impact report "no later than 365 days after" the application is complete, 180 days for a negative declaration, and 90 days to decide that a project is exempt or already covered by a prior review. Those three clocks run in business days, excluding weekends and state holidays; every other deadline in the chapter is in calendar days. The applicant can extend them. The LAO notes that current law also has time limits, but "nothing specific happens if an agency misses" them.
Under Prop 45 something does. Section 21020 lets an applicant, once a deadline passes, demand a meeting or hearing within 60 days at which the agency "shall" make "a final written determination on the available environmental review documentation that has been completed as of the date of the meeting or hearing" and "a final written determination to approve or disapprove the essential project." Compliance with the deadlines is "a nondiscretionary ministerial duty," and the applicant may sue within 90 days to enforce it. The agency keeps the power to say no: "No outcomes on any proposed essential project are preordained by this chapter."
The review: One alternative, standards frozen at filing, comment capped
The second mechanism narrows what the review contains. Section 21025 provides that "the applicant shall develop one proposed alternative to the essential project," which need not be at a different site, and that the EIR "shall only analyze" the project, that alternative and the no-project option; "all additional alternatives beyond those described… are unnecessary." The applicant's alternative "shall be presumed to lessen impacts that the alternative is intended to address" if substantial evidence supports it. Under current law, the LAO says, "the lead agency must develop and consider a range of reasonable alternatives to the project or its location."
Section 21022 fixes the yardstick: impacts are assessed "based on compliance with existing laws," defined as rules "in effect on the date an application for an essential project was submitted," with exceptions for later rules an agency finds necessary to avoid "a specific, adverse life-safety impact" and for building and fire code updates. Section 21021 caps public comment at 20 days for a negative declaration and 45 for a draft EIR, allows extensions only "by a court of competent jurisdiction," bars reopening the period at later hearings, and provides that comments outside those windows, other than oral testimony at a recorded hearing and late comments on issues that could not have been raised earlier, "shall be disregarded and excluded from the administrative record." Current law sets minimum comment periods, not maximums.
Tribal consultation changes too. For essential projects, "California Native American tribe" is redefined to mean a "consulting tribe," one "that appears on the most recent list published by the United States" of federally recognized tribes and is "traditionally and culturally affiliated with the geographic area." The LAO's letter (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250480.pdf) to the Attorney General describes the effect: consultations would be based "on the list of federally recognized tribes, rather than on the longer contact list maintained by the state Native American Heritage Commission." The measure sets its own consultation procedure, with a records search within 20 days and a 30-day response window, and makes agreed mitigation "enforceable conditions of project approval."
The courts: 30 days to sue, 270 to decide, and no power to void the approval
The third mechanism is litigation. Section 21027 requires a CEQA challenge to an essential project to be filed "within 30 days" of the notice of determination and "completed within 270 days, inclusive of original and appellate court proceedings," extendable by up to 90 days at the court's discretion. Section 21026 limits the claims a petitioner can bring to "a public agency's noncompliance with objective existing laws," where objective means "involving no personal or subjective judgment and being uniformly verifiable by reference to an external and uniform benchmark," and limits the court to asking "whether the approval or authorization is supported by substantial evidence in light of the whole record." The LAO's summary of the contrast: "Under current law, the court can use its independent judgment to determine whether an agency appropriately applied CEQA."
The remedy is the sharpest change. If a court finds a violation, "the remedy shall be limited only to prohibiting commencement of the noncomplying part, phase, or activity until the noncompliance is corrected"; "a court may not order or direct… that a public agency rescind its approval," and parts of the project outside the deficiency "shall not be subject to the writ."
A full injunction is available only "upon a showing by clear and convincing evidence that an essential project would have a specific, adverse impact upon public safety" with no feasible mitigation. The administrative record is confined to documents the agency published and to timely comments. Once an approval survives challenge, or the agency files its return to the writ, "no further action or proceeding to challenge the implementation through completion of construction" may be filed. The provisions apply to cases "pending on, or commenced after" the effective date, which, as an initiative, is the fifth day after the Secretary of State certifies the result on December 11.
The measure contains no attorney-fee provision; its only reference to attorneys is a clause directing the Attorney General to appoint independent counsel, with a continuous appropriation, if the Governor and Attorney General decline to defend the act in court.
The cost: High tens of millions a year at first, uncertain after
The LAO's ballot analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm) estimates that "during the first several years, Proposition 45 likely would increase costs for the state and local governments, including state courts," at "the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially exceeding $100 million annually," partly covered by fees on applicants and litigants. Its December 2025 letter had put the same costs at "tens of millions of dollars annually for the first several years" and added that "over the long term… state and local governments likely would experience net savings due to reduced administrative and legal workload," with court effects ranging "from annual savings of up to the tens of millions of dollars to annual costs of up to the low tens of millions."
The ballot analysis is more cautious about the long term, "uncertain, but potentially more significant," in either direction, depending on "how the new procedures change the number of eligible projects that get built and whether those projects have different environmental impacts." It also carries the sentence the No campaign quotes: some agencies "might incur costs to mitigate or respond to" projects approved with "unintended negative environmental impacts."
Proposition 45's author and funders: Nielsen Merksamer, CalChamber and a $226 million committee
The proponent of record is Kurt R. Oneto, a partner at the Sacramento election-law firm Nielsen Merksamer, whose firm bio (https://www.nmgovlaw.com/team/kurt-oneto/) says he "has served as counsel and legal strategist to over 60 ballot measure campaigns." The Attorney General's list (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives/active-measures) shows Oneto as proponent of three measures on this ballot: Prop 45 and the two tax measures, Props 41 and 42, that could cancel the billionaire tax. The California Chamber of Commerce says (https://advocacy.calchamber.com/2026/09/11/calchamber-board-of-directors-announces-positions-on-november-ballot-measures/) it "not only strongly supports Proposition 45… but led the effort to qualify the measure"; the Secretary of State's top-funder disclosure (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/top-funders/2000-top-funders-04-01-26.pdf) for the petition drive names a CalChamber-sponsored committee with "major funding from" Building a Better California, Edison International and the California Building Industry Association.
Building a Better California is the committee behind the campaigns against Prop 40 and for Props 41 and 42, the three measures that decide the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/). Its Cal-Access filings show $226.7 million raised between January 1 and September 19, 2026; the FPPC identifies its top donors as Google co-founder Sergey Brin and venture capitalist L. John Doerr III; it has no public website, and its filer telephone number is that of Nielsen Merksamer's San Rafael office. It has given $10 million to the Yes on 45 committee, the largest single contribution on that side.
The FPPC's October 6 list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/) puts the Yes side at $32.8 million from top contributors across three committees: after Building a Better California come the California Building Industry Association's issues committee ($5.65 million, with KB Home and Lennar as its top donors) and the association itself ($2.25 million), a separate CBIA committee funded by homebuilders ($4.1 million), a committee funded by PG&E ($2.4 million), CalChamber ($2 million), Edison International ($2 million), the California Association of Realtors ($1.5 million), a business PAC funded by California Resources Corporation and PG&E ($1.35 million), and $500,000 each from the hospital association, California Resources Corporation and a committee sponsored by Prologis, the logistics real-estate company. The No side reports $22.2 million: Clean and Healthy California, an environmental political committee, $7.08 million; philanthropist Wendy Schmidt, $5 million; the State Building and Construction Trades Council's committees, $2 million; the Laborers, $1.5 million; Operating Engineers Local 12 and the Iron Workers, $1 million and $1.5 million; and the Center for Biological Diversity, Earthjustice and the Natural Resources Defense Council's action fund in smaller amounts.
The lineup is unusual. The construction trades, which generally support building, are against; so are the Laborers, whose members build the projects the measure covers. The No argument's explanation is the measure's labor provisions and its backers: it "was written by the California Chamber of Commerce and financed by gas and electric utilities and corporate PACs." The Yes argument's coalition includes the California Children's Hospital Association, the California Water Association, American Clean Power, LULAC, the NAACP state conference and the California Taxpayers Association.
The arguments: Red tape versus review
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/arguments-rebuttals.htm) is an affordability case: "Permitting delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new home," it says, and Prop 45 "will help lower rents and mortgages." The campaign's own site (https://yesonprop45.com/) adds a commissioned estimate that the measure would raise housing permitting 18.1% and "add nearly 200,000 homes over ten years." It stresses that "Prop. 45 does not exempt a single project from environmental review" and that "cities and counties retain full authority to approve or deny projects."
The No argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/arguments-rebuttals.htm) is a public-health case: Prop 45 "lets projects move forward with far less scrutiny of their harms to air, water and public health," and "reduces public agency requirements to consider public comments." Its campaign site (https://www.noprop45ca.com/) argues the measure "would fast-track polluting projects like data centers, pipelines, and industrial warehouses." Data centers, pipelines and warehouses are not among the nine categories; the measure's definition does include, for every essential project, "all related and ancillary public, private, and utility infrastructure," and whether that clause lets parts of such projects use the track is a reading the campaigns dispute and the text does not settle. The $75,000, 200,000-home and 639-day figures on the Yes side come from a report the campaign commissioned; all of these are claims, printed in the guide with the standard note that arguments "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
Polling and endorsements on Proposition 45
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of 1,103 likely voters, reading the ballot title, found 49% yes, 46% no and 5% undecided, inside the ±3.8-point margin. No other independent poll has published a Prop 45 result. McClatchy's California editorial board, writing for the Sacramento Bee and four other papers, endorsed (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317475362.html) the measure on October 5; the Bakersfield Californian has also endorsed it; the San Francisco Chronicle's editorial board lists its Prop 45 recommendation as "coming soon," and the Los Angeles Times had not published one as of October 12. The parties have split: the California Democratic Party opposes (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 45 and the California Republican Party supports (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it. Governor Newsom, whose campaign released his positions on 12 of the 14 measures on October 9, has not taken one (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/) on Prop 45; he is "still reviewing" it and Prop 41, his spokesperson told the San Francisco Chronicle (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php).
Proposition 45 after November 3: An immediate rewrite of pending reviews, amendable only by two-thirds
If Prop 45 passes, it takes effect on certification and applies "to all pending and future public agency and judicial review and processes for all essential projects," so applicants with reviews under way could withdraw and resubmit under the new chapter, and pending lawsuits would be subject to its litigation rules. The Legislature could adjust it only by a two-thirds vote that "furthers the purposes" of the chapter. If it fails, CEQA continues as the Legislature has been reshaping it since 2025, exemption by exemption. Either way, Proposition 45 is the first time California voters have been asked to decide the shape of environmental review directly, and the question on the ballot is not whether to review essential projects but how long, how deeply, and with what recourse.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, the FPPC contributor list as of October 6, 2026, endorsements as of October 12, 2026, and polling fielded through September 10, 2026.

Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos KnowledgePanel. Interviews were conducted in

from October 16—22, 2026.

percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups
is larger. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording,
question order, and survey timing.

Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos

preferences. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. Interviewing took place from October
16—22, 2026.
These crosstabs are based on a subgroup of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error, taking design effects
from weighting into consideration, is ±3.8 percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted
sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups is larger. Sampling
error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as
question wording, question order, and survey timing.

PROP 45: The CEQA “Essential Projects” Fast Track (Building an Affordable California Act)
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2045.pdf)

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney General title and summary, December 26, 2025)
Measure’s own name: The Building an Affordable California Act (AG No. 25-0023A1)
Type: Initiated state statute
A vote YES means: A new “essential projects” category (most housing, water, clean energy, medical, public safety, broadband, and transportation projects) gets hard deadlines for CEQA review, a slimmed-down alternatives analysis, and tighter limits on lawsuits, all written into the Public Resources Code [1, Sec. 21013].
A vote NO means: CEQA’s existing review timelines, alternatives requirements, and judicial-review rules stay in place for these projects.
Sponsor/proponent: California Chamber of Commerce. Proponent of record: Kurt R. Oneto of Nielsen Merksamer LLP.
On the ballot because: Qualified by random-sample signature check on June 16, 2026, and certified eligible June 25, 2026. The measure needed 546,651 valid signatures.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0023A1, “Building an Affordable California Act,” Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0023 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-023)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 45 would carve a new fast-track lane through the California Environmental Quality Act for what it calls “essential projects.” It adds a new chapter, Chapter 1.5, to Division 13 of the Public Resources Code, the part of state law that is CEQA. It does not repeal CEQA, and it does not touch the other environmental statutes it names, such as the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the California Coastal Act. What it changes is CEQA’s procedure for a defined set of projects [1, Sec. 1 (21011(h)), 21012-21033].
The measure does three main things for essential projects. First, it puts public agencies on a clock. An agency has thirty days to decide whether an application is complete or the application is deemed complete automatically. Once complete, a lead agency has 365 days to decide whether to certify an environmental impact report (EIR), 180 days to act on a negative declaration, and 90 days to document an exemption. For the 365-day and 90-day review clocks the measure counts only business days, not weekends or state holidays, so the real-world calendar is longer than the raw numbers suggest [1, Secs. 21017-21019, 21028(c)].
Second, it shrinks the alternatives analysis. Today a CEQA environmental impact report must study a reasonable range of alternatives to a project. Under Proposition 45, an EIR for an essential project needs to analyze only the project itself, one alternative developed by the applicant, and the “no project” alternative. The measure declares that any additional alternatives are “unnecessary” and that no agency may require them [1, Sec. 21025].
Third, it narrows the courtroom. A challenger must sue within thirty days of the agency’s notice of determination, the case must finish within 270 days including any appeal, and the court must use the deferential substantial-evidence standard rather than independent judgment. A court that finds a defect may order the agency to redo only the specific study at issue. It “may not order or direct” the agency to rescind its approval of the project, and once a project clears review its later construction and implementation approvals cannot be challenged again [1, Secs. 21026-21027].
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0023A1, “Building an Affordable California Act,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (amended language submitted November 24, 2025)
Key language:
“‘Essential project’ means a project that meets all of the following requirements … The project does not include a jail or other detention facility, or involve the development of a new oil or natural gas production facility.” [1, Sec. 21028(h)]
“A court may not order or direct via writ or any other form of order, injunction, or decision that an agency rescind its approval of the essential project.” [1, Sec. 21027(d)]
What it amends: Adds Chapter 1.5 (commencing with Section 21010) to Division 13 of the Public Resources Code. Because it is an initiative statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, but only in ways that further the measure’s purposes unless it says otherwise. The measure also adds a self-defense clause. If the governor and attorney general both decline to defend it in court, the attorney general must appoint independent counsel, funded by a continuous general fund appropriation [1, Secs. 21010, Section 4].
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, with the initiative filed by attorney Kurt R. Oneto of Nielsen Merksamer. Supporters include the California Building Industry Association, the California Hospital Association, NAACP California, and Pacific Gas and Electric. Opposition is led by environmental organizations, including Sierra Club California, the Planning and Conservation League, and CalBike.
What? A new “essential projects” category covering most housing, water, clean energy, medical, public-safety, broadband, and transportation projects, given fixed review deadlines, a one-alternative EIR, and tighter judicial review. Jails and detention facilities and new oil and gas production facilities are excluded, and by definition Delta conveyance and high-speed rail are left out of the water and transportation categories. [1, Secs. 21013, 21028].
Where? Statewide, applied to all public agencies and written into the Public Resources Code [1, Sec. 21014(d)].
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. It takes effect the day after the election if it passes and applies to applications deemed complete after that date, including projects that withdraw and resubmit to opt in [1, Secs. 21014(f)-(g), 21033].
Why? The proponents frame CEQA delay and litigation as a driver of California’s high housing, energy, and infrastructure costs. Their stated purpose is to “make California more affordable by streamlining and speeding up approval of essential projects” while keeping the state’s other environmental laws intact [1, Secs. 21011-21012].
4. Trade-offs
CEQA review and the lawsuits that follow can add years and cost to housing and infrastructure, and the delay is not evenly aimed at the most polluting projects. The legislature itself has spent recent sessions passing narrower CEQA exemptions for infill housing and other priorities, which shows that the cost-of-building concern is bipartisan and real, not manufactured. Proposition 45 is the broadest response yet because it does by initiative, and across seven whole project categories, what the legislature has done piecemeal.
Every lever the measure pulls to go faster also removes a check that CEQA built in on purpose. Hard deadlines with a “deemed complete” default speed things up, and they also let a clock, rather than a finished analysis, decide when review ends. A one-alternative EIR is cheaper and quicker, and it also means the public document may never study the option that would have reduced harm the most. The substantial-evidence standard and the bar on rescinding approvals cut litigation risk for builders, and they also make it harder for a neighbor or a tribe to stop a project that was genuinely under-analyzed. None of these is a free lunch. Each is a real gain in speed bought with a real reduction in review.
Two things keep this from being a simple pro-building versus pro-environment fight. First, the measure leaves the substantive environmental statutes standing. A project that violates the Clean Water Act or the Endangered Species Act is still illegal under those laws. What changes is CEQA’s procedural review, which is disclosure and analysis, not the pollution limits themselves. Second, the fight will be about the word “essential.” The definitions are broad. “Essential clean energy” reaches carbon-capture and hydrogen infrastructure, and the categories sweep in “related and ancillary” infrastructure as part of the “whole of the project.” How wide that lane runs, and how much of California’s building actually qualifies, is the question the ballot label cannot answer [1, Secs. 21028(f), (h)].
Many CEQA issues are not about acceptable levels of environmental damage. Instead, project opponents use procedural complaints under CEQA to slow down projects that they dislike for reasons having nothing to do with the environment. The proposition’s backers wish to reduce the use of CEQA for such purposes.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It replaces open-ended CEQA timelines with firm deadlines, which can cut the years of delay that raise the cost of housing, water, clean energy, and hospitals [1, Secs. 21018-21019].
The streamlined one-alternative EIR reduces the cost and length of environmental review while still requiring a “no project” comparison [1, Sec. 21025].
Tighter judicial rules, a 270-day case clock, and a bar on rescinding approvals reduce the litigation risk that can stall financing on approved projects [1, Secs. 21026-21027].
The LAO expects state and local governments to see long-run net savings from reduced administrative and legal workload once the system is running.
It leaves the underlying pollution-control statutes—the Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, Endangered Species Act, and Coastal Act—in force, so it narrows CEQA procedure rather than repealing environmental protection [1, Sec. 21011(h)].
Potential risks
A one-alternative EIR and a “deemed complete” default can end review before the analysis is finished, so real environmental or community harms may go unstudied [1, Secs. 21017, 21025].
The bar on rescinding an approval and on challenging later construction approvals sharply limits the public’s ability to stop an under-reviewed project [1, Sec. 21027(d)-(e)].
The “essential project” definitions are broad and include ancillary infrastructure, so fights over what qualifies will be frequent and consequential [1, Sec. 21028(h)].
The LAO estimates implementation costs in the tens of millions of dollars annually for the first several years, with uncertain long-run court effects that could run from savings to added costs.
The self-defense clause commits an open-ended general fund appropriation to hired outside counsel if state officials decline to defend the measure [1, Section 4].
6. Open questions
How much of California’s actual building pipeline meets the “essential project” definition once ancillary infrastructure and the seven categories are counted?
Will the 365 business-day and 90 business-day clocks, which run longer than calendar deadlines, deliver the speed proponents promise?
Does limiting an EIR to one applicant-designed alternative meaningfully weaken the document’s ability to surface lower-impact options?
How will courts read “objective, quantifiable, and written standards” as the new test for a valid CEQA challenge, and how many suits does that screen out?
If the measure passes, how much litigation will target the boundaries of the definitions themselves, and who pays for the state’s defense under the independent-counsel clause?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
CEQA delay is a real driver of what it costs to build housing, water projects, and energy capacity in California. Proposition 45 speeds up those projects by shortening deadlines, shrinking the alternatives study, and limiting lawsuits. The questions are whether faster building is worth a lighter environmental and public review and whether to trust the broad definition of “essential” to stay in its lane.
Every provision that makes a project go faster also removes a check that CEQA put there on purpose. Which risk weighs more: a needed project stalled for years by process and litigation or a harmful project approved before the harm was fully studied?

DOWNWARD ARC — Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects. Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure. But Prop 45 also plunged underwater. Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots. Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers. Opponents of the wealth tax have argued it could eventually be expanded to hit working Californians. Supporters disputed both claims.
PROP 3 HOLDS — The wealth tax’s slide in the polls hasn’t extended to Proposition 3, which would make permanent an existing tax on top earners to fund education. Support for that measure held steady at 58%, a result that may ease union proponents’ fears that opposition to Proposition 40 could spill over to Prop 3.
Those divergent trendlines reflected starkly different political and financial realities. The Prop 3 campaign has raised more than $80 million and faced no funded opposition; the wealth tax effort has operated on a shoestring budget as billionaires spend hundreds of millions of dollars against it. Democrats are largely unified behind Prop 3, while Prop 40 has been extraordinarily divisive within the party.
Prop 40 was not the only SEIU-UHW-championed measure to backslide as opponents piled on. Support for Proposition 44, which would regulate clinics, shrank to just 25% in the face of a $44 million health care industry counteroffensive. In both cases, SEIU-UHW spent millions on qualification but has not followed up with a comparable advertising campaign.
Two billionaire-funded measures designed to torpedo Prop 40 were also on the bubble amid tightening polling: Proposition 41 declined from a 51-44 majority in September to 48-49 this month, and Proposition 42 went from 54-43 to 51-47. Wealthy backers have largely focused on 42, pouring some $65 million into the campaign this month. But the rest of the ballot is looking increasingly predictable as campaigns either held steady or saw polling gaps expand.
THE REST OF THE BALLOT — Voters broadly support two housing bonds (Proposition 1 and Proposition 37), an expansion of the state’s “rainy day” reserve fund (Proposition 2), and an immunology research bond (Proposition 38). A voter ID measure (Proposition 39) and an initiative making it harder to raise local taxes (Proposition 43) are both trailing by double-digit margins. And two measures to institute public election financing (Proposition 4) and overhaul recalls (Proposition 5) remain below majority support despite creeping up to 45%.

WHO WON THE DAY? Prop 40 opponents , who received good news in the PPIC poll.
WHERE’S GAVIN? In Los Angeles, having a fireside chat with California Science Center CEO Jeffrey Rudolph during a media preview of the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center.
TOP READS
SHATTERED RECORDS — Billionaire opponents of California’s proposed wealth tax have spent more fighting it than they ever have on a political cause in the state, according to a POLITICO analysis.
A record $612 million from more than 70 current and former California billionaires is flooding this year’s state elections , nearly half of it to groups working to defeat the wealth tax initiative on Tuesday’s ballot, POLITICO found.
The fight over Prop 40 has brought California’s wealthiest residents — many from its native tech industry — together in an unprecedented show of political coordination, the new data reveals. Tech leaders say the wealth tax has accelerated plans for broader political engagement this cycle, building networks that could be the foundation for future campaigns.
Read the full story from Christine Mui and Sean McMinn here (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/28/billionaires-spending-california-wealth-tax-01137778) .
IN THE COURTS
In this Aug. 30, 2021, file photo, mail-in ballots run through a sorting machine at the Sacramento County Registrar of Voters office in Sacramento, California. | Rich Pedroncelli/AP
ELECTION CLAIM SKEPTIC — A federal judge in California signaled Tuesday that he is preparing to reject the Trump administration’s emergency effort to force the state to set aside and review any votes cast by people on a list of 20,000 registered voters the Department of Homeland Security has identified as likely noncitizens.
After a three-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge David Carter instead said he needed a far more extensive briefing on the matter that would extend well past Election Day. In effect, it’s a defeat for the Justice Department, which had demanded the judge immediately force the state to comply. Carter, a Clinton appointee, said DOJ could prosecute anyone it identifies as casting an illegal ballot.
“Of course no one wants a noncitizen voting. Anybody taking that position, it’s a ridiculous position,” he said.
The judge concluded with a stark warning for DOJ, however, after state officials complained that the Trump administration had made menacing comments about potentially prosecuting election workers who tabulated the votes of noncitizens: “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately.”
Carter said he would issue a formal order Wednesday. — Kyle Cheney
First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli speaks during an announcement at Department of Justice headquarters in Washington on Nov. 19, 2025. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
WHAT’S IN A NAME — A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Bill Essayli is unlawfully acting as a “de facto” U.S. attorney.
Judge J. Michael Seabright , who last year ruled that Essayli was illegally serving in the role (https://www.politico.com/news/2025/10/28/judge-los-angeles-top-federal-prosecutor-illegally-appointed-00626804) of acting U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote that “Essayli—even in his designated role as a Special Attorney and FAUSA—is disqualified from (1) participating in or supervising these cases, or (2) otherwise supervising any attorneys in the handling of these cases.”
Essayli said in a statement that he respectfully disagreed with the ruling.
“The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department,” he said.
Essayli added that the motion was automatically stayed, and that the status quo will likely remain while the DOJ appeals the decision. “Ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court,” he said, “and I look forward to serving in my current role until then.” — Nicole Norman
ELECTION YEAR
Chad Bianco speaks during a California gubernatorial debate hosted by CBS Bay Area and the San Francisco Examiner in San Francisco, Thursday, May 14, 2026. | Godofredo A. Vásquez/AP
RELUCTANT SUPPORT? — It was hardly a ringing endorsement, but Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco , who previously declined to endorse (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) Steve Hilton in the governor’s race after losing the primary, voiced support for his fellow Republican’s candidacy on Tuesday.
“I don’t care if you like him or not. We absolutely need Steve Hilton to win this race for governor,” Bianco said in a video on social media (https://x.com/ChadBianco/status/2115188593425850374?a=NXWO74gQaasvSVU-EC4&s=20).
Bianco in May argued (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) that President Donald Trump ’s endorsement of Hilton (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/04/06/before-trump-backed-hilton-loomer-was-already-at-work-00861205) would hurt the former Fox News host in California. But he urged followers to vote for Hilton in the video, anyway, saying “we need balance” amid Democratic rule.
IN THE PHONE BANK — Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas rallied volunteers at a phone bank supporting Democrat Amy Slavensky , telling them her incumbent opponent Assemblymember Josh Hoover is a “nice guy, but he doesn’t represent this community’s interests.” Outgoing Women’s Caucus Chair Cecilia Aguiar-Curry said electing Slavensky, a former school administrator, was a priority of the caucus. And Assemblymember Gail Pellerin , a former local elections official, instructed callers to encourage voters to drop off their ballots in person rather than by mail, citing concerns about possible Trump administration interference.
“We cannot rely on the United States Postal Service right now because they are under the control of this Trump administration, and we don’t want those ballots to get held somewhere and not in the hands of the elections official,” Pellerin told the volunteers gathered in the Sacramento suburb of Fair Oaks.
The event’s attendance by several Democratic officials, including Assemblymember Patrick Ahrens , underscored the force with which their party is trying to oust Hoover despite his moderate profile and, as Rivas seemed to acknowledge, affable demeanor. The state Democratic Party has poured more than $2 million into defeating the frontline Republican, one of several incumbents it’s trying to oust after losing seats in both chambers of the Legislature last cycle.
Super PACs, including the GOP caucus-aligned Legislative Action Victory PAC and another sponsored by CalChamber, have collectively spent more than $3 million defending Hoover and blasting Slavensky.
LOS ANGELES
Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman speaks during a campaign event on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, in Sylmar, California. | William Liang/AP
POWER PLAY — Frustration over sky-high electricity bills is becoming a flashpoint in the closing days of the Los Angeles mayor’s race, with Karen Bass and her progressive challenger, Nithya Raman , trading blows over utility costs that have soared amid record-breaking heatwaves, Alex Nieves reports for subscribers (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/10/the-la-mayors-race-goes-electric-01137758).
The fracas began early last week after Raman held a press conference alongside frustrated Los Angeles Department of Water and Power customers, where the council member blamed Bass for letting the utility raise electricity and water rates without City Council approval — and promised to audit the department. Bass has responded with promises to lower bills and investigate the city’s climbing utility costs.
The last-minute brawl comes as candidates statewide contend with high electricity prices and broader concerns about the cost of living — an issue (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) which is among voters’ top concerns. California’s electricity rates are the second-highest in the U.S., behind only Hawaii. Read last night’s California Currents (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-currents/2026/10/27/ramans-electric-closing-message-01137445) to see how both campaigns are trying to navigate energy affordability angst ahead of Election Day.
Top Talkers
UCLA SUIT — For the second time this month, the University of California has asked a federal judge to dismiss a lawsuit by the Department of Justice alleging that UCLA failed to properly address antisemitic incidents during protests over Israel’s war against Hamas.

# Prop. 45 seeks to rewrite state environmental law. Here's why San Diegans should care
By Jennifer Van Grove, The San Diego Union-Tribune The Tribune Content Agency
October 25, 2026 4:28 PM
...
Proponents and opponents of the ballot proposition that would rewrite the state's environmental law to expedite the review of so-called essential housing and infrastructure projects agree on one thing: The future of California is on the line.
The existential nature of Proposition 45, the camps say, is either a rare opportunity to make blanket reforms to a law that has hamstrung development and made life in California unaffordable, or it's a snake-in-the-grass attempt to unravel the state's primary way of protecting people from disastrous environmental consequences.
Placed on the November ballot by the California Chamber of Commerce, Proposition 45 seeks to amend the California Environmental Quality Act with new procedures for the environmental review of projects defined as essential.
The state law, enacted in 1970, requires public agencies to study and disclose the environmental impacts of projects before approval.
The proposition, if approved by voters, would allow project applicants to opt into a revised CEQA process that includes tighter, enforceable timelines for permitting and review periods, shorter windows for public input and changes to how courts consider legal challenges.

# Proposition 45
Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects.

## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
Proposition 45 creates new procedures for reviewing certain types of projects that it defines as “essential.”
Figure 1 lists the types of projects eligible for the new procedures.
The proposition (1) tightens time limits for CEQA review, permits, and court challenges; (2) changes parts of the CEQA review process; and (3) changes the court’s review process for CEQA lawsuits.
The proposition gives eligible project applicants the option of using the new procedures or existing procedures.
***Tightens Time Limits for Review and Court Challenges of Eligible Projects.*** Proposition 45 creates more binding time limits for state and local governments to do both CEQA and permitting reviews.
This includes time limits for determining if a project application is complete, finishing the EIR, and granting other types of approvals and permits.

# Opinion: Prop. 45 will take a meat axe to California environmental protections
## CEQA isn't the problem or the solution to building affordable housing or public infrastructure, argues Stanford Law's Deborah Sivas
Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, signs two bills in June 2025 to reform CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act, with the goal of building housing and other projects faster.
By Deborah A Sivas
PUBLISHED: October 26, 2026 at 3:44 AM PDT
...
## Related Articles
Developers are not content to let these substantial CEQA reforms play out.
Instead, they have taken advantage of the “Abundance” movement with an industry-funded voter initiative that goes far beyond streamlining.
Proposition 45 would, among other things, give developers new litigation rights to sue local agencies over even shorter approval deadlines, allow developers to replace the normal “reasonable range of alternatives” that officials must consider with a single, developer-designed onsite “alternative,” and reduce the ability of the public to comment on projects.
...
And here’s the kicker: If passed, Proposition 45 would prohibit future statutory amendments unless they (1) affirmatively “further” the newly-declared statutory purpose of “streamlining and speeding approval of essential projects” and (2) are enacted by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature.
